questions.q: Alex submitted a PR introducing a new feature flag. Ben , the reviewer, commented: 'This flag is too broad; it impacts several modules and increases complexity.' Alex wants to explain that he considered the impact but believes the benefits outweigh the risks. Which of the following email responses is most appropriate?
options: 'Thanks for the feedback, Ben. I've already accounted for the potential impacts in my design.'
'I disagree with your assessment, Ben. The feature flag provides significant value to the user experience.'
'I understand your concern about complexity, Ben. I'll refactor it to be more specific.'
'Ben, could you elaborate on which specific modules are impacted and why you think this is too broad? Providing some context would help me understand your perspective.'
questions.explanation: Option 2 demonstrates a proactive approach by acknowledging the reviewer's concern and stating that Alex has already considered the impact. This shows respect for Ben's feedback while subtly reinforcing Alex's decision-making process. Options C & B are too dismissive or confrontational. Option A lacks detail and doesn't invite further discussion.

questions.q: David is reviewing a PR containing a complex algorithm for data processing. The reviewer, Emily , leaves a comment: 'This algorithm's time complexity is O(n^2). Can you provide more optimization?' David needs to respond professionally and constructively. Which email is best?
options: 'I'm not sure what you mean by O(n log n). Can you explain it to me?'
'This is a perfectly acceptable time complexity; we prioritized scalability over absolute optimization.'
'I optimized it! It's now O(n log n). Thanks for pointing this out.'
'Emily, I appreciate your feedback on the algorithm's complexity. Could you suggest specific areas where I could improve its performance?'
questions.explanation: Option 1 demonstrates that David addressed Emily's concern and improved the algorithm. It shows a willingness to collaborate and highlights the positive outcome of the review. Option 2 is the most constructive, inviting further discussion and specific suggestions for improvement - crucial for code reviews. Options C & B are either boastful or dismissive without demonstrating understanding. Option D frames the question poorly.

questions.q: Frank has submitted a PR containing changes to the user authentication service. The reviewer, Grace , comments: 'I'm concerned about the lack of input validation on this endpoint; it's vulnerable to injection attacks.' Frank needs to respond quickly and appropriately. Which of the following is the most effective response?
options: 'I considered that risk during development and believe the current implementation is sufficient.'
'This is a standard design; we don't typically include input validation for authentication endpoints.'
'Thanks for bringing this to my attention, Grace. I'll immediately add input validation to prevent injection attacks.'
'Don't worry about it, Grace. I've tested it thoroughly.'
questions.explanation: Option 2 shows immediate action and demonstrates an understanding of Grace's concern. It directly addresses the vulnerability and promises to implement necessary security measures. This response is professional, proactive, and crucial when a reviewer identifies a potential issue. Options D & B are dismissive or provide inadequate justification for the lack of validation. Option C is too vague.

questions.q: Henry wants to send a follow-up email regarding a PR that has been stuck in review for three days. The reviewer, Isabelle , hasn't responded. Which of the following emails is most professional and effective?
options: 'Sorry for the inconvenience, Isabelle. Just wanted to ensure you saw my feedback.'
'Hi Isabelle, just checking on the status of this PR. Let me know if you have any questions.'
'Isabelle, I need a response to this PR ASAP! It's blocking my progress.'
'I'm following up on my previous comment regarding the PR. Please let me know when you expect to be able to review it.'
questions.explanation: Option 1 is polite and professional, gently reminding Isabelle of the pending PR without being demanding or accusatory. It invites further discussion and offers assistance if needed. Options B & D are too formal or suggestive. Option C is overly aggressive and could damage the relationship.

questions.q: Jack had a difficult code review with Karen where there were several disagreements. Jack wants to send Karen an email to reset the relationship and move forward constructively. Which of the following emails best achieves this goal?
options: 'I'm not interested in discussing this PR further, Karen. Please respect my decision.'
'I disagree with your assessment of my code, Karen. We can continue to debate these issues if necessary.'
'Karen, I'm still frustrated with your feedback on my PR. It was overly critical and didn't offer helpful suggestions.'
'Karen, I appreciate you taking the time to review my code. Let's put this disagreement behind us and focus on collaborative improvements going forward.'
questions.explanation: Option 2 demonstrates a willingness to move past the disagreement and prioritize collaboration. It acknowledges Karen's efforts while setting a positive tone for future interactions. This approach is crucial for rebuilding trust after a tense review. Options C & B are confrontational and unproductive. Option D is passive-aggressive.

exercises.title: Cold Outreach to Developers
exercises.subtitle: Practise the IT-English phrasing of cold outreach emails to developers: subject lines, personalisation, value-first and clear CTAs.

questions.q: Which is the most effective cold-email 'subject line' for a busy developer?
options: URGENT!!! READ NOW
Quick question about your open-source CLI tool
Hello
Re: Re: Re: meeting
questions.explanation: A specific, relevant subject signals genuine context and respects the reader's time without sounding spammy.

questions.q: Why open with 'personalisation' referencing the recipient's work?
options: To pad the email
To show the message isn't a mass blast and you've done your homework
To hide your name
To add length
questions.explanation: Genuine personalisation shows the outreach is relevant and not a generic blast, improving reply rates.

questions.q: A 'value-first' cold email does what?
options: Asks for a sale immediately
Leads with something useful to the recipient before any request
Demands a meeting
Lists your features only
questions.explanation: Value-first outreach offers something helpful up front, earning attention before asking for anything.

questions.q: What makes a good 'call to action' (CTA) in a cold email?
options: Many vague asks
One clear, low-friction next step, e.g. 'Open to a 15-min call next week?'
No ask at all
A demand to reply now
questions.explanation: A single, easy, specific CTA makes it simple for the reader to say yes.

questions.q: Which closing line is appropriately respectful of a non-reply?
options: Reply or else.
No worries if it's not relevant - feel free to ignore.
You must answer.
I'll keep emailing daily.
questions.explanation: Giving a graceful opt-out keeps the tone respectful and professional.

questions.q: Sarah from our team sent this PR description to the codebase review channel: `Fix: Resolve minor bug in user authentication. Updated JWT validation logic. @JohnDoe - Could you take a look when you have a moment? Thanks!` Which of the following phrases would be most appropriate for Sarah to add *before* her original description to improve the cold outreach aspect of this review request, assuming she's initially contacting John Doe who is known for being very busy?
options: "Please provide feedback on this PR as soon as possible. We're under a tight deadline."
"Hi @JohnDoe, just wanted to flag this minor authentication issue. Any quick thoughts?"
"@JohnDoe, thanks for your time! The JWT validation was causing intermittent errors - let me know if you have any questions."
"Just a small fix related to user auth. This is blocking the new feature release. Could you review it soon?"
questions.explanation: The key here is understanding that 'cold outreach' isn't just about sending an email; it's about efficiently getting someone's attention and making them want to help. Option A sounds demanding and doesn't acknowledge John Doe's potential busyness. Option B is too informal for a code review request, and option C focuses solely on the technical details without offering context or seeking assistance. Option D emphasizes urgency in an overly dramatic way - highlighting the blocking factor isn't necessary and can feel pushy. Option 1 acknowledges John Doe's time constraints while politely requesting his input, which is ideal for a productive interaction.

questions.q: JohnDoe is a senior developer and known for receiving many code review requests. Sarah wants to initially contact him about a JWT validation update within the user authentication PR. Which of the following additions to her original description would be most effective in initiating a productive conversation, acknowledging his time constraints?
options: Insufficient - the account balance is too low...
Please review this PR and let me know if you have any immediate concerns.
This update addresses a minor bug in JWT validation for user authentication; your feedback would be greatly appreciated. @JohnDoe
I've prioritized this fix to ensure optimal security. Please review ASAP, @JohnDoe.
questions.explanation: The best option (2) demonstrates respect for John's time by acknowledging the issue is 'minor' and framing the request as seeking his 'feedback'. This softens the approach compared to a demanding CTA or an overly assertive statement. Options A and D are too direct and potentially overwhelming, while Option B simply requests a review without any context or consideration of John's workload.

questions.q: Mark is reaching out to a senior developer, Alex, about a potential integration with their new API. Mark wants to frame the conversation positively. Which of the following opening lines would be MOST effective in a Slack message? mark@example.com
options: 'Hey Alex, quick question about your API…'
'I've been looking at your API and thought it could integrate really well with our system.'
'Just wanted to see if you had some time for a chat…'
'Regarding the integration… let's discuss.'
questions.explanation: Option 1 directly highlights the potential benefit of the integration - aligning with 'value-first' outreach. Options 2 and 3 are too vague or focus on the request without establishing value. Option 4 is a generic call to action that doesn't immediately demonstrate understanding or interest in Alex's work; developers respond best when they see a clear reason for a conversation.

questions.q: During a stand-up meeting, David wants to briefly explain that he's investigating a performance bottleneck in the user profile service. Which of the following statements is the MOST concise and appropriate for this context? (David is speaking to his team)
options: 'I'm working on optimizing the user profile service, which has been experiencing some latency issues.'
'I've identified a potential performance problem in the user profile service that I'm currently investigating.'
'I'm tackling some performance concerns regarding the user profiles. It's complex…'
'Just wanted to let you know I'm looking into performance with the user profiles.'
questions.explanation: Option 3 is the most direct and concise, suitable for a stand-up update. It clearly states the issue and David's action without getting bogged down in technical details. Options 1 & 2 are overly verbose; option 4 is too informal for a team meeting.

exercises.title: Cross-Team Coordination Emails
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - managing dependencies, feature handoffs, priority conflicts, and multi-team deployment milestones with effective professional communication.

questions.q: Your team is building a feature that depends on the Auth team's new OAuth endpoint - due in Sprint 14. A Sprint 13 retrospective shows Auth is running two weeks behind. Which email opening most effectively coordinates the dependency without creating conflict ?
options: "Hi team - can you give us the endpoint this week? We're blocked."
"Hi Auth team - your delay is blocking our work. When will the OAuth endpoint be ready?"

"Hi [Auth team lead name], I wanted to flag a scheduling dependency ahead of Sprint 14 planning. Our team's session-management feature relies on the new OAuth endpoint currently tracked for Sprint 14. Given the recent timeline shift, I'd like to sync briefly to understand the updated delivery estimate so we can adjust our sprint plan accordingly. Would a 20-minute call work for Thursday?"
"Hi - we need the OAuth endpoint ASAP. Please prioritise this."
questions.explanation: Cross-team dependency emails: name the specific dependency, explain your constraint, propose a low-friction action. Analysis of Option C: ① "I wanted to flag a scheduling dependency" - positions you as proactive, not reactive. You're surfacing the issue before it becomes a blocker, which puts you in a collaborative posture rather than a complaining one. ② Names the specific dependency - "session-management feature" + "new OAuth endpoint" + "Sprint 14" - no ambiguity about what you're asking about. This respects their time (they don't need to chase you for details). ③ "Given the recent timeline shift" - acknowledges the situation without accusation. "Your delay" (Option B) is accusatory even if factually accurate; it triggers defensiveness rather than collaboration. ④ "I'd like to sync briefly to understand the updated estimate" - specific, low-cost ask. You're asking for information, not yet demanding they accelerate. This preserves goodwill. ⑤ Proposes day + duration - "a 20-minute call for Thursday" is easy to accept or counter. Open-ended requests ("let me know when you're free") often delay further. Cross-team email structure: 1. Context: what dependency and when 2. Your constraint: what you need and why 3. Information ask: what you need to know 4. Low-friction action: propose specific next step

questions.q: Two teams - Frontend and DevOps - are collaborating on a shared deployment pipeline config. The Frontend team has been waiting 3 days for a review of their proposed changes. Which follow-up email is most effective?
options: "Hi [DevOps contact name], following up on Monday's message about the pipeline config changes (PR #88). I understand you're managing competing priorities - is there a specific concern or information gap that's blocking the review? I'm happy to set up a 15-minute walkthrough to address any questions. The proposed changes would let Frontend deploy independently and reduce our shared deployment window from weekly to daily. Could you share an updated timeline by [specific date]?"
"Hi - did you see my email? The pipeline changes are urgent."
"Hi DevOps - still waiting for a response. Please review by EOD."
"Hi DevOps - just following up on my email from Monday. No worries if you're busy, just checking in."
questions.explanation: Effective follow-up emails: confirm the reference, surface blockers, explain the value, request a specific response. Why Option A works: ① References the original item - "Monday's message + PR #88" - no ambiguity about which request you're following up on. Reviewers often have 10+ pending requests; specificity helps. ② "Is there a specific concern or information gap that's blocking the review?" - this is the key pivot. Instead of assuming negligence, you're asking whether unblocking is possible. This is psychologically generous and pragmatically smart: sometimes a 5-minute clarification unblocks a week-stalled review. ③ Offers to help, not just request - "15-minute walkthrough" reduces the cost of reviewing. You're solving their problem (understanding the change) not just yours. ④ Restates the business value - "deploy independently + daily vs weekly deployments" - connecting the review to cross-team value creates positive motivation rather than just compliance pressure. ⑤ "By [specific date]" - not EOD (vague), not "soon" (vaguer), but a named date. Specific dates are harder to ignore than relative ones. Option D is too apologetic - "no worries if you're busy, just checking in" signals you don't regard your own request as important, so neither will the recipient. Option C is commanding in tone - in cross-team relationships, "please [do X] by EOD" without context feels like a directive, which people resist.

questions.q: Feature ownership is being transferred between two teams mid-project. Which email most effectively hands off context, responsibility, and open items?
options: "Hi Data team - we're transferring the ETL pipeline to you. Good luck!"
"Hi Data team - everything you need is in the Confluence page. Let me know if you have questions."
"Hi - we're done with the ETL pipeline. It's yours now. See the docs."

"Hi [Data team lead], as discussed in the architecture review last week, ownership of the ETL pipeline service is transferring from the Platform team to the Data team effective [date]. Attached is the runbook, architecture decision record, and a list of 3 open action items with current status. I'd suggest a 30-minute handoff call this week to cover the nuances the runbook doesn't capture. After [date], [Platform contact] will be available for 2 weeks at reduced capacity for knowledge transfer questions. Could you confirm receipt and let me know your preferred time for the handoff call?"
questions.explanation: The professional handoff email: confirm agreement, transfer artifacts, enumerate open items, propose structured knowledge transfer, name the transition owner and period. A feature handoff is a high-stakes communication. Incomplete handoffs are one of the top causes of production incidents in organisations (the receiving team doesn't know about the edge cases, the runbook is outdated, the SME is gone). The email is your SLA documentation. Anatomy of Option D: ① "As discussed in the architecture review" - grounds the email in an agreed decision, not a unilateral announcement. This is important: ungrounded handoffs feel like dumping. ② Effective date - "effective [date]" - no ambiguity about when ownership formally transfers. This is critical for incident response ("who is responsible?"). ③ Lists the artifacts - runbook, ADR, open items with status. The receiving team immediately knows where to find information. ④ Proposes structured knowledge transfer - "30-minute call to cover what the runbook doesn't capture" - demonstrates you've thought about the limits of documentation. ⑤ Named transitional contact - "at reduced capacity for 2 weeks" - professional and honest; the receiving team knows where to escalate and for how long. ⑥ Actionable request - "confirm receipt + preferred time" - two specific actions make the email easy to respond to. Handoff email minimum checklist: ☐ What is being transferred ☐ Effective date ☐ Documentation links ☐ Open items with status ☐ Knowledge transfer offer ☐ Transitional support contact and duration ☐ Explicit confirmation request

questions.q: The Frontend team is blocked by a missing API endpoint the Backend team agreed to deliver. The Backend team says it's deprioritised due to other work. Which email de-escalates while still representing your team's needs effectively ?
options: "Hi [Backend lead] - I want to escalate a priority misalignment that's impacting our sprint delivery. The /api/v2/user-preferences endpoint was agreed for Q3 Sprint 2 (see JIRA ticket #1204). We're currently blocked on 3 of our 5 sprint tasks because of this dependency. I'm not looking to assign blame - I'd like to understand the current priority conflict and explore options: parallel stub development on our side, a reduced-scope version of the endpoint, or a revised delivery date we can plan around. Could we get 20 minutes this week to align? I want to make sure both teams can meet their commitments."
"Hi Backend team - please deliver the endpoint soon. Our team is waiting."
"Hi Backend - you promised to deliver this endpoint two weeks ago. We're completely blocked and this is unacceptable."
"Hi Backend - no problem, we understand you're busy. Let us know whenever you have time."
questions.explanation: Priority conflict emails: name the agreement, quantify the impact, de-personalise blame, offer options, propose a small collaborative action. This is one of the most important cross-team communication skills: asserting your needs without triggering defensiveness or conflict. Breakdown of Option A: ① "Priority misalignment" - reframes the problem as a systems/process issue, not a personal failure. "You didn't deliver what you promised" (Option C) signals blame; "priority misalignment" signals a solvable coordination problem. ② "See JIRA ticket #1204" - having documentation for the agreement is powerful. It's not your memory vs. their memory; it's a shared record. ③ "3 of our 5 sprint tasks" - quantified impact. Numbers make the business case concrete and give the recipient the data they need to re-prioritise internally. "Completely blocked" (Option C) is vague; "3 of 5 sprint tasks" is specific. ④ "I'm not looking to assign blame" - stating this explicitly resets the social contract. It signals you're interested in problem-solving, not confrontation. ⑤ Three options offered - parallel stub development, reduced scope, or revised date. When you offer options, you appear collaborative and reasonable; you're also more likely to get a "yes" to at least one option. ⑥ "Both teams can meet their commitments" - positions your request as mutually beneficial, not a zero-sum ask. Option D is the opposite failure mode - too accommodating. "Whenever you have time" signals you'll absorb the delay indefinitely, which is not professionally sustainable.

questions.q: An infrastructure change requires three teams (Backend, Frontend, DevOps) to coordinate a deployment milestone. Which email structure most effectively organises a multi-team milestone communication ?
options: "Everyone - deploy Monday. Thanks."

"Hi all - Shared deployment milestone: Backend API v3 release / Monday [date] 10:00 UTC. What each team needs to do: • Backend: merge feature flag PR #312 by Friday 17:00 UTC • Frontend: update API client to v3 compatibility layer (see PR #318) by Friday 17:00 UTC • DevOps: prepare rollback runbook and confirm monitoring alerts are updated by Monday 09:00 UTC Single point of contact during deployment: [Name], on-call via #deploy-monday Slack channel Rollback decision owner: [Name], Backend lead Please confirm readiness in this thread by Friday 17:00 UTC. If any team has a blocker, flag it here immediately so we can adjust the plan."
"Hi Backend, hi Frontend, hi DevOps - just a reminder about the deployment on Monday. Please be ready."
"Hi all - the deployment is Monday. Backend needs to do some things. Frontend also. DevOps is handling infrastructure. Let me know if you have questions."
questions.explanation: Multi-team milestone communication requires: specific tasks per team, deadlines per task, roles, confirmation mechanism, and escalation path. When coordinating across three or more teams for a shared deployment, the email must function as an operational brief. The main failure mode is ambiguity - what exactly does each team need to do, and by when? Why Option B works: ① Clear subject / milestone - "Backend API v3 release / Monday [date] 10:00 UTC" - every recipient can immediately verify this is relevant to them and find it by searching later. ② Per-team task list with deadlines - the single most important element. Each team sees exactly what they are responsible for. No team can claim uncertainty about their deliverable. ③ Single point of contact - in multi-team deployments, unclear ownership is how issues fall through the cracks. Naming SPOC + channel removes ambiguity. ④ Decision owner for rollback - in incidents, "who decides to roll back?" needs to be pre-decided and known, not negotiated under pressure. ⑤ "Confirm readiness in this thread by Friday" - synchronous head-count before deployment, async-style. Everyone has a chance to flag blockers before it's too late. Multi-team coordination email structure: ① Milestone name + date/time ② Each team's task + deadline (formatted as a table or bullet list) ③ SPOC and communication channel ④ Decision owner for key choices (rollback, abort) ⑤ Explicit confirmation request with deadline + escalation path

questions.q: John from the Frontend team just submitted a PR to integrate the new user authentication flow. Maria from the Backend team has responded with a comment stating: 'This looks good, but I'm currently focused on resolving critical bugs in the legacy system and don't anticipate being able to review this for at least another week.' Which of the following email responses from you would best manage expectations and maintain a productive working relationship?
options: 'Hi Maria, thanks for your feedback. I understand you're busy with bug fixes. Could you give us an estimated timeframe for when you might be able to review the PR?'
'Thanks Maria, appreciate the update. Let me know when you have some bandwidth'
'Just wanted to check in on the status of my PR. No worries if it's not a priority right now.'

exercises.title: Declining Requests Politely
exercises.subtitle: Practise the IT-English phrasing for saying no by email: cushioning, offering alternatives, explaining briefly and staying professional.

questions.q: Which is the most professional way to decline taking on extra work?
options: No.
Thanks for thinking of me - I can't take this on this sprint as I'm at capacity.
Not my problem.
Ask someone else.
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the request and giving a brief reason declines clearly while staying courteous.

questions.q: Why 'offer an alternative' when declining?
options: To avoid the topic
To stay helpful, e.g. suggesting another time or person, softening the no
To say yes secretly
To delay forever
questions.explanation: Offering an alternative keeps the relationship positive and shows willingness to help where you can.

questions.q: Which phrase appropriately 'cushions' a refusal?
options: Absolutely not.
I appreciate the offer, but I'll have to pass this time.
That's ridiculous.
Why would I?
questions.explanation: A cushion ('I appreciate the offer, but...') softens the refusal and keeps the tone warm.

questions.q: How long should the 'explanation' for declining usually be?
options: Several paragraphs of excuses
Brief - one short reason is enough; over-explaining sounds defensive
No explanation, just refuse
An apology essay
questions.explanation: A concise reason is honest and professional; lengthy justification can seem defensive or invite negotiation.

questions.q: Which closing keeps the door open after declining?
options: Never ask me again.
Do keep me in mind for future projects though.
Forget my email.
I'm done with this team.
questions.explanation: A warm closing preserves the relationship for future collaboration.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'Hey, can you take a look at this? It's pretty urgent!' You (as a developer) are currently swamped with bug fixes and sprint commitments. You need to politely decline the request without appearing uncooperative or dismissive. Which of the following responses is most appropriate in this situation?
options: 'Sure, no problem! I'll get right on it.'
'I'm really busy at the moment and don't have time for new tasks.'
'Could you send me a quick summary of what needs to be done so I can prioritize?'
'Thanks for thinking of me. My current workload is quite high, and I need to focus on resolving existing issues before taking on anything additional.'
questions.explanation: The key here is managing expectations and demonstrating professionalism. Option A sounds overly enthusiastic and doesn't address your capacity. Option B is blunt and could be perceived negatively. Option C attempts to shift the responsibility without acknowledging your own limitations. Option D clearly states your situation, explains why you can't take on more, and politely declines while maintaining a positive tone - showing respect for the reviewer's request.

questions.q: You're working with the requests library to make an API call. The response is returned as a JSON string. You need to parse this string into a Python dictionary. Which method is *most* appropriate for doing this, considering best practices and error handling?
options: - Use json.loads() directly on the raw string.
- Use eval() to execute the JSON string as Python code.
- Use json.loads(response.text) to parse the response text into a dictionary, handling potential errors with a try-except block.
- Use a regex to extract the data from the JSON string directly.
questions.explanation: Using json.loads() is the standard and safest way to parse a JSON string into a Python dictionary. It handles all the necessary parsing logic and avoids potential security risks associated with using functions like eval() , which can execute arbitrary code from an untrusted source. A try-except block would be good defensive programming but isn't *most* appropriate as the initial parsing method.

questions.q: A senior developer on your team sends you this Slack message: 'Hey @john_doe, can you take a look at this? It's pretty urgent!' You check the linked issue and see it's a critical bug in production. What's the *most* appropriate immediate response to acknowledge receipt and indicate you're investigating?
options: - 'Sounds good, I'll get right on it.'
- 'Thanks for letting me know. Let me check it out.'
- 'Okay, thanks for the heads-up. I'm already working on other urgent issues.'
- 'Could you provide more context about why it's urgent?'
questions.explanation: Acknowledging receipt and stating intent to investigate is crucial when someone flags an issue as 'urgent'. Option 2 politely confirms you've seen the message and are taking action. The other options either ignore the urgency or shift responsibility inappropriately.

questions.q: You're writing a PR description for a change that refactors some code. You want to clearly communicate *why* you made the changes and how it improves the codebase. Which sentence is *most* effective in conveying this information concisely?
options: - 'Refactored some code.'
- 'This change improves readability.'
- 'The refactoring was necessary to address performance concerns and improve maintainability.'
- 'I made this change because I felt like it would be good.'
questions.explanation: A good PR description should explain the *reason* behind the changes. Option 3 clearly articulates the rationale (performance & maintainability), providing context for reviewers to understand and appreciate the refactoring. The other options are too vague or lack justification.

questions.q: A teammate asks you to review their code before they push it to the main branch. They say, 'Can you take a quick look when you have a moment?' How long should *your* explanation for declining (if necessary) be?
options: - One sentence.
- A paragraph detailing your entire schedule.
- 30 seconds to briefly explain your current workload and offer a timeframe for review.
- An email outlining all the reasons you're busy.
questions.explanation: While politeness is key, a brief explanation that acknowledges the request and provides a realistic timeframe demonstrates professionalism. 30 seconds allows you to convey your current workload without over-explaining or appearing dismissive. A longer explanation can seem overly formal or defensive.

questions.q: You've just declined a request from a colleague to help with a task that you are already fully committed on. You want to end the conversation in a way that maintains a positive working relationship and leaves the door open for future collaboration. Which closing statement is *most* appropriate?
options: - 'No thanks.'
- 'I'm really busy right now, so I can't help you.'
- 'That sounds interesting, but I have too much on my plate at the moment. Perhaps we could revisit this next week?'
- 'Sorry, I don't have time.'
questions.explanation: Offering to revisit the request in the future demonstrates willingness to help if circumstances change and preserves a positive working relationship. It's polite, proactive, and doesn't completely shut down communication.

exercises.title: Professional IT Email Structure
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - identifying email parts (subject · context · CTA · closing), writing effective subject lines, and choosing the right professional tone.

questions.q: A colleague sends you this email: "Hi, I was wondering if maybe we could potentially fix the bug that's been causing some issues with the login flow at some point before the next release if it's not too much trouble?" Which part of a professional email is most broken here?
options: The call to action (CTA)
The greeting
The subject line (implied)
The closing line
questions.explanation: The main problem is the call to action - the actual request is buried in uncertainty ("wondering if maybe", "potentially", "some issues", "at some point", "if it's not too much trouble"). A professional email CTA should be: specific ( what needs to happen), scoped ( which bug), and time-bound ( by when ). Better: "Could you prioritise the login-flow bug before the v2.4 release on Friday?" The five parts of a professional email: Subject · Greeting · Context/Body · Call to Action · Closing.

questions.q: You need to email the team that the production deployment is delayed until tomorrow. Which subject line is most effective?
options: "DELAYED: Production deployment - rescheduled to 2026-03-17 09:00 UTC"
"Re: the deployment"
"Update"
"Hi everyone, just letting you know the deployment won't happen today"
questions.explanation: " DELAYED: Production deployment - rescheduled to 2026-03-17 09:00 UTC " - A good subject line should be a one-line summary that lets the reader decide urgency without opening the email. Best practices for IT email subjects: ① Start with a status keyword if relevant: DELAYED / ACTION REQUIRED / FYI / RESOLVED / REMINDER. ② Name the system or project. ③ Add a time or date if actionable. Option C is too vague. Option B assumes the reader knows the context. Option D is a full sentence - subject lines should be fragments, not sentences.

questions.q: Read this email and identify which labelled section is the Context (background) rather than the Call to Action. "[A] Hi Sam, [B] The staging environment has been returning 503 errors since the overnight deployment at 02:00 UTC. [C] Could you roll back the deployment and confirm once staging is stable? [D] Thanks, Alex"
options: Section A
Section B
Section C
Section D
questions.explanation: Section B is the Context: it states what happened ( 503 errors ), which system ( staging environment ), and since when ( since the overnight deployment ). Section A is the Greeting. Section C is the Call to Action ("Could you roll back…"). Section D is the Closing. The structure Greeting → Context → CTA → Closing is the baseline for clear professional emails. Good context sentences answer: What happened? Where? Since when? Who is affected? - so the reader has everything they need before the ask.

questions.q: You need to tell a client that a feature they requested cannot be delivered this sprint. Which response is most professionally worded?
options: "We can't do that."
"No, that's out of scope."
"I'm so sorry but we really can't manage to fit this in right now, hopefully next time!"
"Unfortunately, the requested feature falls outside the current sprint scope. We've added it to the backlog and will prioritise it for the next release cycle."
questions.explanation: Option D is the most professional: it gives a reason ("outside current sprint scope"), takes clear ownership, and provides a next step ("added to backlog, prioritised for next release"). Professional declining emails: ① Acknowledge the request. ② Give a brief reason. ③ Offer an alternative or next step. Option B is too blunt - correct but sounds dismissive. Option A is short but gives no reason or next step. Option C over-apologises and sounds informal ("hopefully next time" is vague and unprofessional).

questions.q: Which subject line correctly follows professional IT email conventions for an action-required message?
options: "I need you to look at something important"
"Architecture"
"ACTION REQUIRED: Review architecture proposal - deadline 2026-03-20"
"Please review the architecture proposal for the new microservices migration"
questions.explanation: " ACTION REQUIRED: Review architecture proposal - deadline 2026-03-20 " follows three conventions: ① Status prefix ( ACTION REQUIRED ) - tells the reader immediately that a response is expected. ② Clear topic ( architecture proposal ) - no need to open the email to know what it's about. ③ Deadline in subject line - a date in the subject is the single most effective thing you can do to get a timely response. Option D is good but lacks an urgency signal and deadline in the subject. Option B is too brief. Option A is vague and informal.

questions.q: Sarah : 'Hey team, just ran some tests on the new API endpoint. Response time is consistently around 8 seconds for requests with over 100 items. I've attached the full report. Let me know if you have any questions!' Which of the following best describes Sarah's email and how it should be revised to improve clarity and professionalism for a code review discussion?
options: Incorrect - Sarah's email is too technical and jargon-filled for a general audience. She needs to simplify the language and explain the implications of the response time in terms that everyone understands - e.g., 'This could impact user experience.'
Correct - Sarah's email is perfectly clear and concise, providing all necessary information. The report attachment serves as sufficient evidence of the issue.

Partially Correct - The email includes data but misses an opportunity to suggest next steps. Sarah should include a brief summary of her findings and propose a potential cause for the slow response time, such as database queries or network latency.
Insufficient - The email lacks specific recommendations for improvement based on the data. It simply presents the raw response time metrics without context or actionable insights.
questions.explanation: Sarah's email is adequate but lacks strategic direction for a code review. A good code review update shouldn't just present raw metrics; it should *interpret* them and suggest actions. The explanation highlights the need to frame the response time within a broader context-user experience-and propose potential causes or areas for investigation, which are crucial steps in productive technical discussion. It's important to move beyond simply reporting data and towards actionable insights.

questions.q: Maria sent this email to the team regarding a recent code change: Subject: Fix - Bug in User Profile Update Hey guys, Just pushed the fix for the bug where user profiles weren't updating correctly. It was a simple typo in the database query, and I've added comments to the code explaining the fix. Let me know if you have any questions. Thanks, Maria
options: Maria's email is acceptable, but she should include a link to the code change in Git for easy access. Including 'simple typo' might be too casual.
Maria's email should include a detailed technical explanation of the database query and the potential consequences of not fixing it.
Maria's email is perfect as is - it's concise and clearly communicates the issue and resolution.
Maria's email lacks detail; she needs to specify which bug was fixed, what the impact of the bug was, and provide a summary of the fix. The subject line is also too vague.
questions.explanation: The best response acknowledges that Maria's email isn't *bad*, but could be improved for clarity and professionalism in a code review context. While concise is good, providing context - specifically mentioning the user profile issue and its impact - strengthens the message. The subject line needs to be more specific than 'Fix - Bug in User Profile Update'. Including a link to the change would also be beneficial, but adding excessive technical detail isn't necessary for this stage.

Insufficient - The email lacks specific recommendations for improvement based on the data. It simply presents the raw response time metrics without context or actionable insights.

Incorrect - Sarah's email is too technical and jargon-filled for a general audience. She needs to simplify the language and explain the implications of the response time in terms that everyone understands - e.g., 'This could impact user experience.'
Correct - Sarah's email is perfectly clear and concise, providing all necessary information. The report attachment serves as sufficient evidence of the issue.
questions.explanation: Sarah's email is adequate but lacks strategic direction for a code review. A good code review update shouldn't just present raw metrics; it should *interpret* them and suggest actions. The explanation highlights the need to frame the response time within a broader context-user experience-and propose potential causes or areas for investigation, which are crucial steps in productive technical discussion. It's important to move beyond simply reporting data and towards actionable insights.

questions.q: Maria sent this email to the team regarding a recent code change: Subject: Fix - Bug in User Profile Update Hey guys, Just pushed the fix for the bug where user profiles weren't updating correctly. It was a simple typo in the database query, and I've added comments to the code explaining the fix. Let me know if you have any questions. Thanks, Maria
options: Maria's email is perfect as is - it's concise and clearly communicates the issue and resolution.
Maria's email lacks detail; she needs to specify which bug was fixed, what the impact of the bug was, and provide a summary of the fix. The subject line is also too vague.
Maria's email is acceptable, but she should include a link to the code change in Git for easy access. Including 'simple typo' might be too casual.
Maria's email should include a detailed technical explanation of the database query and the potential consequences of not fixing it.
questions.explanation: The best response acknowledges that Maria's email isn't *bad*, but could be improved for clarity and professionalism in a code review context. While concise is good, providing context - specifically mentioning the user profile issue and its impact - strengthens the message. The subject line needs to be more specific than 'Fix - Bug in User Profile Update'. Including a link to the change would also be beneficial, but adding excessive technical detail isn't necessary for this stage.

questions.q: John : 'Hey team, I've just run a load test on the new authentication service. The average response time is currently 3 seconds under normal traffic, but spiked to 15 seconds when we simulated 50 concurrent users. I've attached the full report.' Which of the following best reflects John 's intention in this message?
options: To simply share the results of a load test without context.
To ask for feedback on the authentication service's design.
To inform the team about a critical performance issue and provide supporting data.
To request immediate assistance with scaling the service.
questions.explanation: The core purpose is to highlight a significant problem (spike in response time) with accompanying evidence. Options D and B are too strong - it's not an immediate emergency request or a casual report. Option C accurately captures the message's intent: reporting a critical issue with data backing it up. Note that a good follow-up would include suggestions for improvement, but this email focuses on alerting .

questions.q: You're drafting a Slack message to your team regarding an unexpected error in the payment processing module. The error is intermittent and only affects transactions over $100. Which of the following options provides the most effective communication?
options: 'Hey everyone, we're seeing some intermittent errors with payments > $100. Investigating… fingers crossed it's just a weird edge case.'
'Just noticed a bug in the payment system - let's troubleshoot together!'
'URGENT: Payment processing failing! Fix ASAP!'
'Payment processing module experiencing an issue. Please investigate and report any further occurrences.'
questions.explanation: This option strikes the right balance between urgency (highlighting the problem) and avoiding panic. Option C is too alarming and unproductive. Option B lacks detail and doesn't clearly communicate the scope of the issue. Option A uses informal language which might be acceptable in Slack but isn't suitable for a formal update. Option 2 provides context, acknowledges the potential nature of the problem, and invites collaboration .

exercises.title: Escalation Emails
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - opening with impact, quantifying business cost, security escalation framing, and requesting decisions with deadlines.

questions.q: You need to escalate a blocked infrastructure request to your VP. Which email opening is most effective?
options: "I wanted to reach out because I'm having some issues with a database request that is taking too long."
"Hi [VP name], I'm sorry to bother you but I've been trying to get help with something for a while and nobody is responding."
"Please help. The database team is not responding to my ticket and the situation is getting worse."
"Escalation: Database quota increase for orders-db - blocked 11 days. Impact: write latency is degrading 4% daily. Immediate decision needed."
questions.explanation: An escalation email opening must state what is blocked, how long it has been blocked, the business impact, and what decision is needed - immediately, before any pleasantries. Option D hits all four in two sentences. Option B opens with an apology ("sorry to bother") which undermines urgency and buries the issue. Option A is vague ("some issues", "too long"). Option C names a team in a blame-attributing way ("not responding") - frame the obstacle as a process gap, not a people failure.

questions.q: Complete this escalation: "This ticket _____ (block) two sprint deliverables. I _____ (already/escalate) to the infrastructure team lead on May 19 with no response. At current trajectory, the release _____ (miss) its June 3 deadline."
options: has blocked / already escalated / will miss
is blocking / have already escalated / will miss
is blocking / escalated already / is going to miss
blocks / already escalated / misses
questions.explanation: Is blocking (present continuous) describes an ongoing, active obstruction happening right now - the correct tense for a current blocker. Have already escalated (present perfect) links a past action (the May 19 escalation) to the present situation - it shows a prior step was taken and the problem persists. Will miss (future simple) is a factual prediction about a future deadline. Option C ("is going to miss") is grammatically possible but weaker - "will miss" is more decisive and confident in an escalation context.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly quantifies the impact in an escalation email?
options: "This is causing significant delays for our team and our customers are unhappy."
"Every day of delay costs approximately $4,200 in SLA credits and delays the Q2 milestone by one day."
"The situation is getting quite serious and we really need this resolved."
"Multiple teams are affected and this is a very high priority issue."
questions.explanation: Escalation emails should quantify impact in business terms that a VP or director can act on : cost per day, SLA breach amounts, milestone slippage in concrete days. Option B does exactly that - $4,200/day in SLA credits and a 1:1 day slip on Q2. This gives the escalation recipient everything they need to justify action to their own stakeholders. Options A, C, and D use vague intensifiers ("significant", "quite serious", "very high priority") - these are not actionable because they don't tell a decision-maker what the actual cost of inaction is.

questions.q: You've been asked to escalate an unresolved security vulnerability. What must your escalation email include that other escalations don't typically require?
options: A longer list of everyone you've already talked to.
A request to assign your most senior engineer to the task.
A CVSS score or severity classification, the attack surface, and whether the vulnerability is already public (CVE published or actively exploited).
A statement that this is "extremely urgent" repeated multiple times for emphasis.
questions.explanation: Security escalations require standardized severity framing that lets recipients understand risk without domain expertise. The CVSS score (e.g., CVSS 9.1 / Critical) is universally understood. Attack surface scoping ("publicly reachable API endpoint") tells leadership who is at risk. Public disclosure status (CVE published, active exploitation in the wild) drives legal and PR considerations. Together these let a VP or CISO decide whether to invoke the incident response process immediately or schedule a fix. Repeating "urgent" (Option D) doesn't add information - severity scores do.

questions.q: Choose the best closing for an escalation email: "I _____ (request) a decision by EOD Thursday so we _____ (can/keep) the June 3 release on track. I _____ (be/happy) to join a 15-minute call today or tomorrow to discuss options."
options: have requested / can keep / will be happy
am requesting / can keep / am happy
request / can keep / am happy
would request / could keep / would be happy
questions.explanation: Request (present simple) is the most direct and professional register for a formal written request - it is declarative and confident. Can keep (present simple modal) expresses a condition: given the decision, the release can stay on track. Am happy (present simple) is the standard English phrase for expressing willing availability. Option B ("am requesting") uses present continuous which sounds more tentative and informal. Option D uses "would" throughout, which makes the email sound too conditional and soft for an escalation that needs action. Option A uses present perfect ("have requested") which refers to the past - but this is a new request being made right now.

questions.q: Team Lead just sent you this Slack message: 'Hey, the new API endpoint is timing out consistently for users in Europe. We've increased the timeout but it's still happening. Can you look into it?' You need to escalate this issue to the DevOps team and highlight the potential impact on user experience. Which of the following email subject lines would be most effective?
options: Europe User Impact - API Request Errors
Urgent: API Issue in Europe
Requesting Assistance with API Performance
API Endpoint Timeout - Europe
questions.explanation: The best subject line immediately communicates the problem's location (Europe) and its potential significance (Urgent). Options D and A are too generic. While 'Requesting Assistance' is polite, it doesn't convey the severity or focus of the issue. Using 'Urgent' in the subject line signals the need for immediate attention and prioritization, which is crucial when escalating a production-level problem.

questions.q: Sarah , a junior developer, has been working on integrating a new third-party library into the core application. During code review, her team lead, David , left a comment highlighting potential performance issues with the library's heavy data processing. Sarah responded by saying 'I'll look into it later.' David replied in Slack: 'This is impacting user latency significantly. Can you provide an estimated timeframe for resolving these bottlenecks?'. Which of the following email drafts would be most appropriate for Sarah to send to David, escalating the issue and requesting support?
options: 'David, I'm aware of your feedback regarding performance. I'm currently prioritizing other tasks and will address this when my bandwidth allows.'
Insufficient - simply acknowledging the comment without detailing further investigation is not proactive.

'Hi David, thanks for raising this. The library's data processing is causing noticeable latency spikes, particularly during peak usage times. I've started profiling the code and expect to have a preliminary report with potential solutions within 24 hours. Could you please advise on any specific metrics you'd like me to focus on?'
'I'm working on it. The library is complex, so it might take a while.'
questions.explanation: The correct option demonstrates proactive communication and provides concrete steps being taken. It acknowledges the issue's severity (latency), outlines Sarah's investigation plan (profiling), and sets a realistic timeframe for reporting back. Options B and A are passive and don't show urgency or a commitment to resolution, while option C is too vague and doesn't offer specific details. Option D is completely unhelpful - it avoids the issue entirely.

exercises.title: 📧 Follow-up Email After a Job Interview
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - write a professional follow-up that leaves a positive impression: the right timing, subject line format, body structure, tone calibration, and closing phrases.

questions.q: You finished a software engineer interview at a startup on Tuesday afternoon. You felt it went well. When should you send a thank-you / follow-up email?
options: Immediately by text or call while you're still in the building
After one week - give the hiring team time to interview all candidates first
Within 24 hours - ideally the same evening or by Wednesday morning
Do not send one - follow-up emails are seen as intrusive in tech hiring
questions.explanation: Send within 24 hours - the same evening or next morning is ideal. This timing shows genuine interest and professionalism while the interview is still fresh in the interviewer's mind. The thank-you email also gives you one more brief touchpoint to reinforce a positive impression. Why within 24 hours? ① The interviewer likely met several candidates - your email arrives while they still remember specific things you said ② Hiring decisions in tech startups can move fast - sometimes within 2 days ③ It demonstrates follow-through and initiative, both valued in engineering roles What if you wait a week? The email loses relevance - the team has moved on, and it may even look like an afterthought. Are follow-up emails intrusive? No - a professional, concise thank-you is standard practice. The only scenario where you might skip it: if the recruiter explicitly said "no need to follow up." Format: Email is standard; avoid LinkedIn DM or text/call unless those channels were used for the interview arrangement.

questions.q: You interviewed for a Senior Backend Engineer role. Which subject line is most appropriate for your follow-up email?
options: "Re: My Application"
"Did I get the job?"
"Following up on our meeting"
"Follow-up: Senior Backend Engineer Interview - [Your Name], Tuesday 18 March"
questions.explanation: "Follow-up: Senior Backend Engineer Interview - [Your Name], date" is correct. A strong interview follow-up subject line has three elements: ① Signal word - "Follow-up:" tells the reader immediately what kind of email this is ② Role + company context - "Senior Backend Engineer Interview" - if the recruiter has multiple open roles, this disambiguates ③ Your name + date - makes the email easy to find and forward (e.g., to the hiring manager) Why the others fail: "Did I get the job?" - too casual, puts pressure on the reader, and may irritate a busy recruiter "Re: My Application" - too vague; doesn't signal what stage you're at or what you want "Following up on our meeting" - "meeting" is imprecise for an interview context; also lacks your name and date Pattern to remember: Follow-up: [Role Title] Interview - [Your Full Name], [Day DD Month] Some candidates add the company name too, which is helpful if they're applying to multiple places simultaneously: "Follow-up: Backend Engineer Interview - Acme Corp - [Name]"

questions.q: You're drafting a follow-up email after a positive technical interview at a fintech company. Which content is most appropriate for the body of the email?
options: Negotiate your salary upfront and ask the interviewer to share your expected offer
Express gratitude for the interviewer's time + reference one specific moment from the interview + restate your interest in the role
Request detailed feedback on your answers for each technical question you were asked
Attach an updated CV and explain that your skills have improved since the interview
questions.explanation: Gratitude + specific reference + restated interest - this three-part structure creates a professional, personalised follow-up that stands out from generic emails. Why this combination works: ① Gratitude - "Thank you for taking the time to speak with me" - basic professional courtesy; never skip it ② Specific reference - "I particularly enjoyed discussing the microservices migration challenge - it made me think about [X]" - this proves you were engaged and listened, not just going through the motions. It also reminds the interviewer of a positive moment ③ Restated interest - "I'm very interested in joining the team and working on [specific project/challenge mentioned]" - signals forward motion without pressuring the interviewer What NOT to include in this email: • Salary negotiation - premature; wait until an offer is made • Updated CV - implies you sent something below par originally; don't draw attention to weaknesses • Demand for detailed feedback - this feels entitled; you can ask for brief feedback if you're rejected, but not before the decision Length: 3-4 short paragraphs maximum. Interviewers are busy - a wall of text undermines the impact.

questions.q: A colleague shares this draft follow-up email: "Hi Sarah, just checking if you've made any decisions yet? I'm very excited and I really need this job. I have financial obligations and really hope I'm selected. Please let me know as soon as possible." What is the most significant problem with this email?
options: It is too short - a follow-up email should have at least five paragraphs to demonstrate commitment
It did not attach an updated CV or portfolio link
The greeting should be formal: "Dear Ms. [Last Name]" rather than "Hi Sarah"
It reveals desperation, creates emotional pressure on the interviewer, and weakens your positioning as a candidate
questions.explanation: Desperation and pressure are the core problem. "I really need this job," "I have financial obligations," and "please let me know as soon as possible" all shift the emotional burden onto the reader and undermine the candidate's professional positioning. Why this damages your chances: ① It creates discomfort - interviewers are not responsible for your financial situation; making them feel that pressure creates a negative emotional association with your application ② It signals desperation - candidates who communicate from a position of need are perceived as less selective - which paradoxically makes you look less desirable ③ "Please let me know ASAP" - implies urgency that isn't yours to set; the hiring timeline belongs to the company The professional alternative: "Hi Sarah, thank you for the opportunity to interview for the backend role on Tuesday. I enjoyed the conversation about the data pipeline architecture challenges. I remain very interested in joining the team. I look forward to hearing about next steps at your convenience." Tone calibration: Professional follow-up = warm + concise + interested + patient What to avoid = desperate + pressuring + overly personal + demanding

questions.q: Which closing sentence is most appropriate for a follow-up email to a software engineering recruiter or hiring manager?
options: "Let me know if you decided. Thanks."
"Please do not hesitate to reach out if you need any additional information. I look forward to hearing from you."
"I'll follow up again on Monday if I haven't heard back by then."
"I expect a decision by the end of this week."
questions.explanation: "Please do not hesitate to reach out if you need any additional information. I look forward to hearing from you." is the professional standard for a follow-up email close. It achieves three things without overstepping: ① Opens a door for the recruiter - "do not hesitate to reach out" signals availability and willingness to provide more (code samples, references, technical clarification) ② "I look forward to hearing from you" - signals interested anticipation without demanding a timeline ③ Leaves the next move with the hiring team - correct, because it belongs there Why the others fail: "I'll follow up again on Monday" - announces a follow-up before the original email has been read; can irritate a busy recruiter and signals impatience. If you want to follow up again, do it - but don't announce it in advance "I expect a decision by end of week" - you don't set the hiring timeline; this reads as pushiness "Let me know if you decided. Thanks." - grammatically awkward ("if you decided" → should be "once you've made a decision") and far too casual for a professional context Full closing formula: Thank you again + availability offer + forward-looking close + professional signature (name, LinkedIn, phone)

questions.q: You spent the last week reviewing a colleague's pull request for a new microservice. The PR was initially rejected due to several minor styling inconsistencies and a lack of comprehensive unit tests. After discussing the feedback with your colleague and helping them address these issues, the PR was finally merged. Now, you're drafting a brief follow-up message to your team lead about this process. Which of the following options best describes the tone and content for your email? Option A: 'Hi [Team Lead], Just wanted to confirm that the microservice PR has been merged. It was a bit tedious, but we got there.' Option B: 'Hi [Team Lead], Following up on the recent microservice PR ( #1234 ). I provided feedback and support to my colleague in addressing the styling issues and adding unit tests, leading to successful merging. I'm happy to discuss this further if needed.' Option C: 'Hey [Team Lead], Just letting you know the PR is done. Don't worry about it.' Option D: 'Hi [Team Lead], The microservice PR was merged! I think the code quality has improved significantly thanks to my review.'
options: 'Hi [Team Lead], Just wanted to confirm that the microservice PR has been merged. It was a bit tedious, but we got there.'

'Hi [Team Lead], Following up on the recent microservice PR ( #1234 ). I provided feedback and support to my colleague in addressing the styling issues and adding unit tests, leading to successful merging. I'm happy to discuss this further if needed.'
'Hey [Team Lead], Just letting you know the PR is done. Don't worry about it.'
'Hi [Team Lead], The microservice PR was merged! I think the code quality has improved significantly thanks to my review.'
questions.explanation: The correct answer (B) demonstrates professional communication within a development team. It acknowledges your contribution clearly and concisely while highlighting the positive outcome - successfully merging the PR through collaborative effort. Options A and C are too informal and don't convey appropriate appreciation or offer further discussion. Option D is overly assertive about code quality, which isn't always the best approach in a professional setting; it's better to focus on the process and the successful resolution.

questions.q: You've just finished a technical interview for a DevOps Engineer role at a cloud services provider. During the interview, you discussed your experience with Kubernetes and CI/CD pipelines. The interviewer emphasized the importance of automation and monitoring within their environment. You want to send a brief follow-up email to reinforce your interest and highlight your relevant skills. Which of the following emails best achieves this goal? Option A: Subject: DevOps Engineer Application Hi [Interviewer Name], I enjoyed learning more about the DevOps role at [Company Name] and your team's focus on automation. I'm confident my skills in Kubernetes and CI/CD align well with your requirements. Please let me know if you need any further information. Option B: Subject: Following up - DevOps Engineer Role Just wanted to reiterate my strong interest in the DevOps position. I'm a fast learner and eager to contribute to [Company Name]. Option C: Subject: DevOps Interview Feedback Thank you for taking the time to speak with me yesterday about the DevOps Engineer role. I appreciate the opportunity to discuss my experience with Kubernetes and CI/CD. Option D: Subject: Interested in DevOps Role I'm very interested in the DevOps Engineer position at [Company Name]. I think I would be a good fit for your team.
options: Option A
Option B
Option C
Option D
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of professional email etiquette in a technical context. Option C is the best response as it directly references the conversation's focus on automation and monitoring - demonstrating you listened and are aligned with their priorities. Options D and A are too generic and lack specific details to showcase your skills effectively, while Option B simply expresses interest without providing any value or reinforcing key takeaways from the interview.

exercises.title: Incident Reports & Post-mortems
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - writing SEV-level notifications, impact statements, blameless root cause analysis, and time-bound action items.

questions.q: A production service has gone down. You need to send an initial incident notification. Which opening sentence is most effective?
options: "Hi team, there seems to be some kind of issue with the payment service, we are looking into it."
"The payment service database connection pool appears to be exhausted based on initial logs."
"I'm sorry to bother everyone, but it looks like we might have a problem with payments."
"SEV-1 | Payment Service Down | Impact: ~3,000 users unable to checkout | Since: 14:22 UTC"
questions.explanation: Incident notifications must lead with severity, system, impact, and start time - the four facts stakeholders need first. Use the format: SEV-[N] | [System] [Status] | Impact: [user/business scope] | Since: [time UTC] . Option A is vague ("some kind of issue"). Option C sounds apologetic rather than informative. Option B starts with a probable cause before confirming the impact - cause analysis belongs in a later update, not the first notification.

questions.q: Complete the impact statement in this incident report: "Users _____ (affect) by this incident are those attempting checkout with a saved payment method. Orders using PayPal _____ (not/affect)."
options: being affected / not affected
are affected / are not affected
affected / are not affected
that are affected / are not affected
questions.explanation: Use present simple passive to describe the current state of the incident: "Users are affected" (right now, ongoing). This is more direct and natural than the participial phrase "users being affected" or the relative clause "users that are affected". The negative, "are not affected" , clearly scopes the impact - limiting scope is a key part of professional incident communication (it reduces panic and helps triage).

questions.q: You are writing the root cause section of a post-mortem. Which wording follows blameless post-mortem principles?
options: "The incident was caused by John, who deployed a misconfigured environment variable to production."
"Someone pushed a bad config. The CI pipeline should have caught this but didn't."
"The root cause was developer error - a misconfigured environment variable was deployed.
"A misconfigured environment variable was deployed to production, bypassing the environment validation step in CI."
questions.explanation: Blameless post-mortems describe system and process failures , not individual ones. Option D is correct: it names the technical artefact ( misconfigured environment variable ), the action ( deployed to production ), and the process gap ( bypassing environment validation in CI ). Option A names an individual - this violates blameless principles and discourages psychological safety. Option C still uses "developer error" (blame). Option B is informal and lacks precision.

questions.q: You're writing action items at the end of a post-mortem. Which action item is written correctly?
options: "We should probably add better monitoring."
"Improve logging." (owner: backend team)
"Make sure this never happens again by adding more checks across the board."
"Add alerting on connection pool exhaustion - threshold: >80% capacity. Owner: @alice. Due: 2024-02-15."
questions.explanation: Post-mortem action items must be specific, measurable, assignable, and time-bound . Option D is the only one that meets all four criteria: it specifies the exact technical action ( alerting on connection pool exhaustion, threshold >80% ), names an owner ( @alice ), and has a deadline ( 2024-02-15 ). Options A and C use vague language ("probably", "more checks across the board"). Option B lacks a deadline and an individual owner - "backend team" is not an owner.

questions.q: Choose the best phrase to complete a resolution update: "The incident _____ at 15:47 UTC after we _____ the connection pool limit and _____ the affected instances."
options: resolved / increasing / restart
got resolved / did increase / did restart
was resolved / increased / restarted
has been resolved / have increased / have restarted
questions.explanation: Past simple passive ( was resolved ) is standard for incident resolution announcements - the incident is a specific completed event. The subsequent actions ( increased the connection pool limit, restarted the affected instances ) are also past simple - a completed sequence of actions in the past. Present perfect ( "has been resolved" ) would work in a real-time update ("we're happy to report…"), but past simple is cleaner for formal post-mortem writing. The "did + base verb" construction (Option B) is emphatic and sounds unnatural here.

questions.q: Sarah : "I've just reviewed the PR and noticed a potential race condition in the payment processing module. It seems like we're updating the database concurrently without proper locking." Which of the following responses would be most appropriate for Mark , the lead developer, to send back on Slack?
options: Insufficient - simply stating the issue doesn't convey urgency or next steps.
Okay, I understand. Please send me a detailed technical report outlining the specific code involved and the steps to reproduce the issue.
Excellent! This is a clear and concise description of the problem. Let's schedule a meeting immediately.
That's a good observation, Sarah . Could you elaborate on the potential consequences if this race condition isn't addressed before deployment?
questions.explanation: The best response acknowledges Sarah's observation while also prompting for further detail. The incorrect options either minimize the severity (Insufficient), offer overly positive feedback without seeking more information (Excellent!), or shift responsibility without encouraging deeper investigation (send a detailed report). A good developer communication focuses on understanding the *impact* of the issue and planning next steps, as highlighted by option 2.

questions.q: Mark : "Okay, Sarah. Thanks for flagging that. Let's investigate the locking mechanism in more detail and ensure we're using appropriate transactions to prevent data corruption."
options: Insufficient - simply acknowledging the issue without offering further action.
Accepting blame - immediately takes responsibility for the potential race condition.
Too vague - lacks specific steps or a timeline for resolution.
Promising immediate fix - suggests a quick solution without proper investigation.
questions.explanation: This response is most appropriate because it acknowledges Sarah's concern and proposes a clear next step: investigating the locking mechanism. It avoids taking blame (option 3) and provides a concrete action - further analysis - rather than offering a simplistic or vaguely worded solution. Options A and B are too passive, while option C doesn't demonstrate any proactive engagement with the issue.
