questions.q: 'The service is experiencing intermittent high latency. Users are reporting slow response times when accessing the API endpoint /users . Initial investigation suggests a potential bottleneck in the database query execution.' Which of the following responses best acknowledges the issue and requests further information from the developer, aligning with effective code review practices?
options: 'The API endpoint is overloaded - try scaling up your servers.'
'It's just a minor issue. Don't worry too much about it.'
'Can you provide more detail about the specific users affected and the exact response times you're seeing? Also, please check the database query logs.'
'This is unacceptable! Fix it immediately!'
questions.explanation: This option directly requests crucial details (affected users, response times) and asks for log examination - key elements of a productive code review. The other options are overly aggressive, dismissive, or offer irrelevant technical advice. Focusing on specific data points allows the developer to pinpoint the root cause efficiently.

questions.q: 'Hey team, we have an outage! Users can't access our website. Please investigate ASAP.' Receiving this message in a Slack channel, what is the MOST appropriate follow-up response to request further details and coordinate efforts?
options: 'Can you provide the current status of the outage (e.g., estimated time to resolution)? Also, who is responsible for investigating?'
'This is a disaster! We need to escalate this immediately!'
'Just let me know when it's fixed.'
'Okay, thanks for letting us know. We'll look into it.'
questions.explanation: Requesting the outage status and identifying the responsible team member are critical for effective incident response. The other options are passive or escalate unnecessarily. A clear request for information ensures everyone understands the situation and their role in resolving it.

exercises.title: Common IT Email Scenarios
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - practise writing professional English for real IT situations: maintenance windows, vendor escalations, project kickoffs, deadline follow-ups, and first contact with enterprise clients.

questions.q: You need to notify users of a planned 2-hour maintenance window on Saturday at 02:00 UTC. Which email is most professional and complete?
options: Subject: [Scheduled Maintenance] Service Downtime - Saturday 22 March, 02:00-04:00 UTC Dear [Product Name] users, We will be performing scheduled infrastructure maintenance on Saturday 22 March from 02:00 to 04:00 UTC (approx. 2 hours). During this window: • The [Product Name] API and dashboard will be unavailable • All scheduled jobs will be paused and will resume automatically after the window • No data will be lost We recommend completing any critical tasks before 01:45 UTC. We will send an update when maintenance is complete. If you have questions, contact support@example.com. Thank you for your understanding, [Company] Operations Team
Subject: Downtime this weekend FYI the platform will be down Saturday night for about 2 hours. Let us know if you have questions.
Subject: Maintenance Hi, we will be doing maintenance on Saturday. The site will be down.

Subject: Important Notice Regarding Our Platform To Whom It May Concern, Please be advised that our technical department will be conducting necessary system maintenance procedures during the forthcoming weekend. We apologize for any potential inconvenience this may cause to your workflow and operations.
questions.explanation: Maintenance notification email anatomy: A maintenance notification email must let the reader answer three questions in When exactly? What will be affected? What do I need to do? Why Option A is correct: ① Subject line pattern: [Scheduled Maintenance] Service Downtime - Saturday 22 March, 02:00-04:00 UTC - the [tag] allows users to filter; the date+time+timezone are in the subject so the reader doesn't even have to open the email to get the key fact ② Specific date, time, timezone, duration - "02:00-04:00 UTC (approx. 2 hours)" - never write "Saturday night" for an international audience; UTC is the professional standard ③ Impact scoped clearly - bullet list: what's unavailable, what's paused, what's preserved. The reader can quickly confirm their use case is or isn't affected ④ Concrete recommendation - "complete critical tasks before 01:45 UTC" - gives users something to act on ⑤ Follow-up commitment - "send an update when maintenance is complete" - closes the communication loop ⑥ Contact path - support@example.com - specific, not "email us" Maintenance email subject formula: [Scheduled Maintenance] [Service Name] Downtime - [Day DD Month], [HH:MM-HH:MM TZ] Option C: No timezone, no date, no impact details - inadequate Option D: Overly formal and vague - "forthcoming weekend" and "necessary system maintenance procedures" give no actionable information Option B: Too casual, missing timezone and impact scope for a professional customer-facing notice

questions.q: Your application depends on a third-party payment API. It has been throwing 503 errors for 4 hours, affecting 30% of your transactions. Your customers are noticing. Which escalation email to the vendor is most effective?
options: Subject: API not working Hi, your payment API has been down for 4 hours and our customers are complaining. Please fix it.

Subject: [URGENT] 503 Errors - Payment API - 4h Ongoing Incident - Account #A-88821 Dear Support Team, We are experiencing a production incident caused by persistent 503 errors from your payment API (endpoint: /v2/charge). The issue began at approximately 09:15 UTC today and has been ongoing for ~4 hours. Impact: • ~30% of transaction attempts are failing at checkout • Estimated revenue impact: ~$8,000 last 4 hours • Customer-facing error rate has increased by 400% We have confirmed: our API keys are valid · authentication is working · the issue is isolated to /v2/charge · other endpoints (/v2/refund, /v2/customers) are responding normally. Requested actions: 1. Confirm whether you are aware of a service degradation 2. Provide an ETA or incident ticket number 3. Confirm whether a workaround or fallback endpoint is available Our SLA requires
To Whom It May Concern, I am writing to express our concerns regarding the reliability of the payment processing service that we have been utilising. We have been experiencing difficulties.
"Your API keeps failing. We are losing thousands of dollars. This is completely unacceptable. We will cancel our contract unless this is fixed in the next hour."
questions.explanation: Vendor escalation email - professional incident communication: When a third-party service is causing a production incident, your escalation email has two goals: get the problem solved quickly, and create a formal record. Angry emails (Option D) often slow support response times. Vague emails (Options A, C) give the vendor nothing to work with. Why Option B is correct - structural breakdown: ① Subject line - [URGENT] tag + specific error code + duration + account number. Support teams triage by subject line; every detail here means faster routing ② What, when, how long - "503 errors from /v2/charge, since 09:15 UTC, ~4 hours ongoing" - pinpoint context with zero ambiguity ③ Business impact in numbers - "30% of transactions failing, ~$8,000 impact, 400% error rate increase" - converts a technical issue into business urgency the vendor can escalate internally ④ What you've already ruled out - "API keys valid, auth working, isolated to /v2/charge" - this is crucial; it proves the problem is on their side and prevents a slow back-and-forth of basic troubleshooting ⑤ Numbered action requests - "Confirm awareness · ETA or ticket number · fallback endpoint" - clear, specific, and easy to address one-by-one ⑥ SLA reference - "SLA requires Escalation formula: [URGENT/P1] [Service] [Error] - [Duration] - [Account/Ref] Body: What broke · Since when · Business impact · What we ruled out · Requested actions · SLA reference

questions.q: You are a tech lead kicking off a new project with a team of 6 engineers who haven't worked together before. Which kickoff email sets the right foundation?
options: This is the project kickoff email for Project Helios. Please note that the project scope, timeline, and deliverables are as follows: [Scope: to be defined]. [Timeline: 8 weeks]. [Deliverables: to be defined]. Please review the attached documentation and revert at your earliest convenience.
"Hi all, welcome to the team. Please review the Jira board and get started on your tasks. Let me know if you have questions."
"Hey everyone! So excited for this project!! 🎉 Check out the Jira board and let's do this. Reach out if you have ?s!!"

Subject: [Project Helios] Kickoff - Team Intro + First Steps Hi team, Welcome to Project Helios - I'm [Name], tech lead for this project, and I'm looking forward to working with all of you. **Quick introductions** - brief backgrounds: • [Name] (you) - Tech lead, previously on the auth platform team • [Name] - Backend, specialises in distributed systems • [Name] - Frontend, React + Figma • [Name] - QA lead • [Name] - DevOps / infra • [Name] - PM, driving the roadmap **Project context:** We're building a real-time notification service for our B2B customers. Deadline: first demo in 8 weeks. Stakeholders: CTO + 2 customer accounts. **Important links:** • Jira board: [link] · GitHub repo: [link] · Figma mocks: [link] · Slack channel: #helios • Architecture proposal (please comment by Friday): [link] **First-week priorities:** 1. Review architecture doc and leave comments by Friday 2. Set up local dev environment (README: [link]) 3. Join kickoff call: Thursday 14:00 UTC ([calendar link]) Feel free to reach out directly if anything is unclear. Happy to be on this with you all. [Name]
questions.explanation: Project kickoff email - professional team communication: A kickoff email does four things: establishes who everyone is, sets context for the project, gives people immediate links and actions, and establishes the leader's communication style. It's often the first shared record of the team's structure. Why Option D is correct - what each section does: ① Subject line - [Project Helios] Kickoff - Team Intro + First Steps - the project name in brackets makes it searchable; "Team Intro + First Steps" tells recipients to read this one carefully ② Short intro sentence - own name + role + brief welcoming tone. Professional but warm. ③ Team roster with roles - 6 people in role bullets. New teams waste days figuring out "who owns what" - this removes that ambiguity on day 1 ④ Project context in 2 sentences - what it is, when the demo is, who the stakeholders are. Every engineer should understand the business context of what they're building ⑤ Link list - Jira, GitHub, Figma, Slack, architecture doc - no one has to ask "where is the repo?" ⑥ Numbered first steps with deadlines - "review by Friday, set up env, join Thursday call" - specific, actionable, time-bounded ⑦ Warm close - "happy to be on this with you all" - professional relationship-building Option B: No context, no intros, no links - fails the new team completely Option A: Bureaucratic template language ("revert at your earliest convenience", "[to be defined]") - gives no actual information Option C: Too informal - excessive emoji and enthusiasm don't substitute for structure Kickoff email formula: Subject: [Project Name] Kickoff - [What the email contains] Body: Brief welcome · Team roster with roles · Project context (what + timeline + stakeholders) · Links · First-week actions with deadlines

questions.q: You need to follow up with a colleague who missed a deadline for delivering a code review you depend on. The review is now 3 days late and is blocking your PR. Which email is most professional?
options: Subject: URGENT - PR Review Overdue - Please Respond PR #412 is now 3 days overdue. I've been waiting since Tuesday. This is blocking the sprint. I need a response as soon as possible. Please confirm receipt of this email.
"Hi [Name], just wanted to remind you about that review."

Subject: PR Review - [#412 auth-refactor] - Follow-up Hi [Name], I'm following up on PR #412 (auth-refactor), which I sent for review on Tuesday. It's now been three days and I'm blocked from merging until I have sign-off. I understand you've had a busy sprint - totally fine if this slipped through. Would you be able to review it today or tomorrow? If you're overloaded, I'm happy to ask [Name] to cover, or split the review. Just let me know. Thanks, [Name]
"Why haven't you reviewed my PR yet? This is really holding up the project."
questions.explanation: Follow-up on a missed deadline - professional tone and structure: Missed deadlines between colleagues happen constantly in software teams. How you follow up affects both the outcome and the working relationship. The goal is to get the task done without damaging trust. Why Option C is correct: ① Specific subject with ticket reference - "PR Review - #412 auth-refactor - Follow-up" - the reviewer can find the PR immediately without asking ② Timeline stated without accusation - "sent for review on Tuesday, now three days" - the facts speak for themselves ③ Personal impact without drama - "I'm blocked from merging" - explains why this matters without catastrophising ④ Charitable framing - "totally fine if this slipped through" - assumes the best, preserves the relationship ⑤ Specific asks with flexibility - "today or tomorrow?" gives a timeframe; offering alternatives (reassign or split) shows you're solution-focused, not just complaining ⑥ No pressure tactics - no "URGENT", no "please confirm receipt", no guilt Option D: Accusatory ("why haven't you") - damages the relationship and puts the other person on the defensive Option B: Too vague - "just wanted to remind you" gives no specifics and is easy to ignore Option A: "URGENT" in the subject for a 3-day slip is disproportionate; "please confirm receipt" is passive-aggressive Missed deadline follow-up formula: Subject: [Task/Ticket] - Follow-up Body: What I sent · When · Impact of waiting → charitable framing → specific timeframe ask → alternatives/flexibility Tone calibration: Day 3: polite follow-up as in Option C Day 5: add escalation signal ("I may need to reassign to keep the sprint on track") Day 7+: loop in manager with a neutral "FYI I'm still blocked on X, escalating visibility"

questions.q: A potential enterprise client reached out asking for a meeting to evaluate your company's API platform. You have never spoken to them before. Which reply is most professional?
options: "Hi! Thanks for reaching out! We'd love to chat!! Please let us know your availability!!"
"Sure, happy to chat. What time works for you?"
"Dear Sir/Madam, We acknowledge receipt of your communication and wish to express our sincere appreciation for your interest in our organisation's application programming interface platform."

Subject: Re: API Platform Evaluation - Happy to Connect Dear [Name], Thank you for reaching out - it's great to hear from [Company Name]. I'd be glad to set up a call to walk you through our API platform and understand your evaluation requirements. Could you let me know your availability for a 30-minute call this week or next? I'm generally available [Mon-Thu, 10:00-17:00 CET] and I'm happy to adjust for your timezone. In the meantime, you might find our API documentation and a brief platform overview helpful: • API docs: [link] • Platform overview: [link] Looking forward to speaking with you. Best regards, [Name] [Title] | [Company] [Phone] | [Email]
questions.explanation: First outreach reply to a potential enterprise client: A first reply to a potential enterprise client is a critical first impression. It signals professionalism, competence, and the communication standard they can expect from your organisation. Both extremes - overly formal (Option C) and too casual (Option B, Option A) - miss the target. Why Option D is correct - element by element: ① Subject line - "Re: API Platform Evaluation - Happy to Connect" - echoes their topic + signals positive response; enterprise clients often triage email by subject ② "Dear [Name]" - not "Hi!", not "Dear Sir/Madam" - standard professional first contact when you know the name ③ Warm acknowledgement in one sentence - "great to hear from [Company Name]" - personalised, not generic ④ Re-states the purpose clearly - "walk you through our API platform and understand your evaluation requirements" - enterprise sales involves understanding their needs, not just pitching ⑤ Specific scheduling offer - 30-minute call + availability window + timezone + willingness to adjust. This removes the scheduling dance ⑥ Pre-meeting resources - links to API docs and platform overview give them something to review before the call, which signals you value their time ⑦ Professional sign-off - name, title, company, phone, email - enterprise contacts need all of this Option A: Multiple exclamation marks read as unprofessional in enterprise B2B communication Option C: Awkward over-formality ("We acknowledge receipt of your communication") - outdated register that signals bureaucracy Option B: Works for an internal colleague; too informal for a first external enterprise contact Warm-professional first reply formula: Subject: Re: [Their topic] - [Positive signal] Dear [Name] → thank + personalise → confirm intent + value prop → scheduling offer with window + timezone → optional: pre-meeting resources → warm close → full professional signature

questions.q: Sarah just submitted a pull request for the user authentication module. During her code review, David left a comment suggesting she refactor the `validate_token` function to use a more robust cryptographic library. He also pointed out a potential vulnerability related to improper input validation. Sarah needs to respond to David's feedback and propose a plan for addressing these concerns. Which Slack message would be most appropriate?
options: I appreciate your feedback, but I'm currently focused on other features and won't be addressing this right now.
Insufficient - the authentication module is working fine.
Okay, I'll look into using a more robust library. Thanks for the suggestion!
David, thanks for the detailed review! I agree; let's prioritize upgrading the cryptographic library and adding input validation. Can we schedule a quick chat to discuss the best approach?
questions.explanation: The key here is acknowledging David's feedback constructively while outlining a plan of action. Option 2 demonstrates understanding and willingness to improve without immediately dismissing the concerns. Options B and A are dismissive or unresponsive. Option D shows collaboration and provides a clear next step - scheduling a discussion - which is crucial in a code review scenario. It's important to show you've considered the feedback and are moving forward.

questions.q: John reported a critical bug in the production service this morning. The error logs indicate a race condition during database updates. He's requested assistance from the on-call team to investigate and implement a fix. Draft an email to the on-call team summarizing the issue and requesting immediate action. Consider that the on-call team is already handling several urgent incidents.
options: 'Hi Team, We have a critical bug in production. Please investigate ASAP.'
'Please investigate the recent errors reported by monitoring systems. A fix should be deployed as soon as possible.'
'Team, there's an issue with the service. Can someone look into it?'

'Subject: Urgent - Production Bug - Race Condition Detected Dear On-Call Team, We've identified a race condition affecting the database during updates in production. John has provided detailed logs and is available to collaborate. Requesting immediate investigation and resolution. Thanks, DevOps'
questions.explanation: This email provides a clear and concise summary of the critical situation, including the specific error (race condition), the affected component (database updates), and the reporter's availability for collaboration. Option 1 is too vague; options 2 clearly outlines the problem, assigns responsibility, and requests immediate action - crucial when dealing with production incidents. Options 3 and 4 are insufficiently detailed and lack urgency.

questions.q: Alex submitted a PR with the following description: 'Fixed bug where users couldn't log in after password reset. Used bcrypt for password hashing.' You are reviewing this PR and notice that Alex hasn't provided any tests for the new password hashing implementation. You also see a comment from another reviewer suggesting a more secure salt generation strategy. Which response to Alex best communicates your concerns and guides him towards improving the PR?
options: insufficient - Alex needs to add unit tests before merging.
excellent - Alex has provided a complete solution with detailed documentation; no further action is needed.
good - Alex should consider the salt strategy suggestion but doesn't need immediate testing.
perfect - the description is clear and concise, covering all requirements.
questions.explanation: The key here is to balance constructive feedback with acknowledging good work. Option 2 incorrectly praises the PR as 'perfect' without highlighting critical omissions like testing. Options 1 and 3 are too directive - Alex might disagree with needing *more* tests immediately. Option 4 overstates the completeness of the solution, neglecting the important security considerations raised by the other reviewer. A good response acknowledges the positive (the bcrypt implementation) while gently prompting further action regarding testing and the salt strategy.

questions.q: You've just received a pull request from Ben for the new image processing service. He's included a basic implementation that converts images to JPEG format using a simple resizing algorithm. During your review, you notice he hasn't documented any error handling or considered potential performance bottlenecks. Another reviewer pointed out that the current approach could easily lead to memory exhaustion with large images. Which response to Ben is most effective in guiding him towards a more robust and scalable solution?
options: Correct - Ben's implementation meets the basic requirements for converting images to JPEG format.
Insufficient - the image processing service isn't currently deployed to production.

Incorrect - While error handling and performance are important, Ben's initial focus was simply to get a working image conversion service running; further optimization should be addressed in subsequent iterations.
Incorrect - Ben has done a great job, focusing on core functionality and performance is secondary at this stage.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of prioritizing tasks within a code review. The key here is recognizing that Ben's initial goal was functionality - getting *something* working. While error handling and performance are crucial considerations for production systems, they aren't the primary focus during an initial implementation. Option B is incorrect because it misinterprets the purpose of a code review; option A provides a completely wrong assessment of Ben's work. Finally, option D incorrectly suggests that performance isn't important, while option C misses the opportunity to constructively guide Ben towards better practices.

exercises.title: LinkedIn Messages for IT Professionals
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - how to write effective LinkedIn messages in job search contexts: connection requests, responding to recruiters, referral requests, rewriting weak messages, and handling vague InMails.

questions.q: You want to connect with a senior engineer at a company you'd like to work for. The LinkedIn connection request note has a 300-character limit . Which message is most effective?
options: "Hello! I am a software developer with 5 years of experience in Python, JavaScript, React, Node.js, Docker, and AWS. I am currently looking for new opportunities and would be glad to connect with you to discuss potential openings at your company."
"Hi there! I'm looking for a job in tech and noticed you work at a great company. Are you hiring? Please check my profile."
"Hi, I found your profile and would like to add you to my professional network. Thanks."
"Hi Alex, I've been following your posts on Kubernetes scaling - your talk at KubeCon was helpful. I'm a backend engineer exploring SRE roles. Would love to connect."
questions.explanation: LinkedIn connection request - what works and why The default message ("join my network") is ignored by most professionals. A personalized note immediately sets you apart. Why option D is best: ✅ Addresses the person by name (personalizes immediately) ✅ Shows specific research - mentions a real talk/post ✅ States who you are in one sentence ✅ Gives a clear, reasonable reason to connect ✅ Fits within the 300-character limit Problems with the others: ❌ Option C: Generic - could be sent to anyone; gives no reason to accept ❌ Option A: Way over 300 characters; lists skills instead of building connection; sounds like a spam application ❌ Option B: Asks for a job immediately - transactional and presumptuous on first contact Template structure for a good connection request: "Hi [Name], [specific reason you know them / common ground]. I'm a [role] interested in [relevant area]. Would love to connect." Key principle: Give before you ask. Show genuine interest in them first.

questions.q: A recruiter sends you a LinkedIn InMail about a Senior DevOps role. You're interested but currently in your notice period - you can start in 3 weeks. Which reply is most professional?
options: "Thank you for contacting me. I am interested in this opportunity and I am available immediately. Please send me more details about the salary and benefits."
"Hi, sorry but I'm currently employed. Maybe reach out in a few months. Thanks."
"Yes I am interested! Call me anytime. My number is [phone number]. Please send interview details ASAP."
"Thanks for reaching out! I'm interested but I'm currently serving my notice period. I'll be available in 3 weeks - would that timeline work for your process?"
questions.explanation: Responding to recruiter InMail - best practices Recruiters send many InMails. A professional, clear response that addresses their main question (availability) gets a quick, positive reply. Why option D is best: ✅ Acknowledges the message warmly but briefly ✅ States clearly you're interested (answers their primary question) ✅ Gives concrete timeline information proactively ✅ Asks a clarifying question to move the conversation forward ✅ Professional tone - not too formal, not too casual Problems with the others: ❌ Option B: Brushes them off unnecessarily - 3 weeks is a very short wait, not months ❌ Option A: Claims to be "available immediately" when you aren't - dishonest; also jumps straight to salary before a conversation is established ❌ Option C: Sharing your phone number publicly in a message is a privacy risk; "ASAP" sounds demanding Key vocabulary for job-search LinkedIn messages: • "I'm currently serving my notice period" or "I'm wrapping up my current role" • "I'd be available from [date]" - specific dates are better than "in a few weeks" • "Would that timeline work for your process?" - invites them to continue the conversation • "Happy to discuss further" / "I'd welcome a call" - professional next step offers

questions.q: You want to ask a former colleague to refer you internally at their current company. They worked with you on a project 2 years ago. Which message is best?
options: "Hey [Name]! Hope you're doing well. I saw [Company] is hiring for a Senior Frontend Engineer - that's the kind of role I've been targeting. We worked together on the design system at [Previous Company] - I'd love your honest take on whether it's a good fit. If you think so, would you be open to referring me? No pressure at all!"
"Hello [Name], I am writing to formally request that you provide a reference for my application to [Company] as a Senior Frontend Engineer. Kindly confirm your availability to proceed."
"Hi! Can you refer me for the frontend job at your company? I need a job urgently."
"Hi, remember we worked together? I want to apply to your company but I don't know how. Can you help me? What is the interview process like? Also, can you forward my CV to the hiring manager?"
questions.explanation: Referral request - getting it right Asking for a referral is sensitive. You're asking someone to put their name behind you. The right message makes it easy to say yes. Why option A is best: ✅ Warm opener - reconnects genuinely before the ask ✅ Mentions the specific role (reduces work for them) ✅ References specific shared work - shows it's not a mass message ✅ Frames the referral as their honest judgment ("if you think so") - reduces pressure ✅ Explicit "no pressure" - makes it easy to decline gracefully ✅ Conversational LinkedIn tone - not stiff, not too casual Problems with the others: ❌ Option C: No context, "urgency" makes it about your needs, not the opportunity ❌ Option B: Overly formal for LinkedIn - reads like a legal letter; impersonal ❌ Option D: Too many vague questions; asking them to forward your CV is overstepping on first contact Referral etiquette checklist: • Reconnect briefly before the ask • Name the specific role clearly • Remind them of your shared context • Give them an easy way to say no • Don't ask more than one favor at a time • Follow up with a thank-you regardless of their answer

questions.q: Rewrite this weak LinkedIn message to make it stronger: "Hello. I am a developer. I want to work at your company. Can we talk?" Which rewrite is most effective?
options: "Hi there! I'm a developer and I noticed you work at [Company]. Is your company hiring? Please check my LinkedIn profile for my full experience."
"Dear Sir/Madam, I write to express my strong interest in employment opportunities at your esteemed organization. My enclosed curriculum vitae details my qualifications."

"Hi [Name], I'm a full-stack developer with 4 years of experience in React and Node.js. I've been following [Company]'s work on real-time collaboration tools - it's the kind of technical challenge I'm actively looking to work on. Would you be open to a 15-minute conversation?"

"Hello! I am a highly motivated, results-driven developer with exceptional communication skills and a passion for innovation. I believe I would be a valuable asset to your organization. I look forward to your response."
questions.explanation: The anatomy of a strong LinkedIn message The original message ("Hello. I am a developer. I want to work at your company. Can we talk?") fails on every dimension: no specifics, no shared context, no value to the reader. Why option C is best: ✅ Names the person ✅ Gives a specific role and concrete skills (not just "developer") ✅ Shows research into the company's specific work ✅ Connects your interest to your skills - relevant fit ✅ Makes a specific, low-commitment ask (15 minutes) instead of "can we talk?" Problems with the others: ❌ Option D: All buzzwords ("highly motivated", "results-driven", "passion for innovation") - meaningless, sounds like a form letter ❌ Option A: Asks "are you hiring?" - recruiter/connection can't know this; go to the careers page instead ❌ Option B: Overly formal, possibly AI-generated corporate letter tone - wrong register for LinkedIn messages The "I-you-we" principle for networking messages: • Mention them first (what caught your attention about their work) • Then tell them who you are (one specific sentence) • Then suggest what we could do (a clear, low-friction next step)

questions.q: A recruiter sends you this InMail: "Hi - I saw your profile and I think you'd be great for a role. We're not able to share details publicly yet, but it's at a top tech company. Interested?" What is the most professional and safe reply?
options: "Hi! I'm definitely interested. Here is my updated CV attached. Please share it wherever needed. My current salary is [salary] and I'm looking for at least 20% more."
"No thanks, I only talk to recruiters who share the company name up front."
"Hi, thank you for reaching out. I'd like to know more before deciding - could you share the role title, company name, and location? I'm generally open to the right opportunity."
"Sure, sounds great! What's the company? I'm ready to interview whenever."
questions.explanation: Responding to vague recruiter InMails Recruiters sometimes send vague InMails to gauge interest before revealing the client company. This is standard practice - but you should ask for basic details before committing. Why option C is best: ✅ Polite and professional tone ✅ Asks for minimum required information to make a decision ✅ Doesn't commit to anything yet ✅ Leaves the door open ("generally open to the right opportunity") - positive signal without over-committing ✅ No private information shared yet Problems with the others: ❌ Option D: "Ready to interview whenever" before knowing the role, salary, or company - over-commitment with no information ❌ Option B: Unnecessarily dismissive - vague first messages are common; politely asking for details is the professional response ❌ Option A: Never share your CV in a LinkedIn message before you know who you're talking to (spam risk, data privacy). Never volunteer current salary in a first message - it reduces your negotiating position Information to ask for in a first reply: • Role title and level (Senior, Staff, Lead?) • Company name (or sector if under NDA) • Location / remote policy • Salary range (you can ask politely) "I'd like to understand the role better before moving forward - could you share the role title and whether there's flexibility on location?"

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey Mark , just finished the latest pull request. A few minor style issues - mostly around whitespace and naming conventions. Let's discuss these in detail when you have a moment."
options: acceptable - Sarah is politely acknowledging the feedback without offering to collaborate.

exercises.title: LinkedIn Networking Messages
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - connection requests, conference follow-ups, job inquiries, and cold email subject lines for engineers.

questions.q: You want to connect with a senior engineer whose open-source library you use. Which LinkedIn message is most effective?
options: "Hi, I'm a software engineer looking to expand my network. Please connect with me!"

"Hi [Name], I've been using your react-query-cache library for six months - the stale-while-revalidate implementation saved us significant re-architecture time. I'd love to connect and follow your work."
"Hi, your profile looks very interesting. I work in tech too. Let's connect!"
"Hi, I'd like to add you to my professional network on LinkedIn."
questions.explanation: An effective cold connection request is specific, gives value to the recipient, and states why you want to connect . Option B names the exact library, gives a concrete use case (six months of use), mentions a specific technical decision it enabled (saved re-architecture), and states a genuine reason to connect (follow their work). The recipient learns that their work had a real impact - this makes accepting the request feel worthwhile. Options D and A are LinkedIn default messages or generic. Option C has no specific information - "your profile looks interesting" says nothing.

questions.q: Complete this networking message to a conference speaker: "I _____ (attend) your talk on distributed tracing at QCon last week. Your approach to sampling rate trade-offs _____ (change) how I _____ (think) about observability costs. I _____ (be/grateful) to connect."
options: attended / changed / am thinking / would be grateful
attended / has changed / think / would be grateful
have attended / has changed / think / would be grateful
was attending / changed / think / am grateful
questions.explanation: Attended (past simple) - the conference was a completed event in the past. Has changed (present perfect) - the change happened in the past but has a current result: your thinking is different now as a result of the talk. Think (present simple) - a current ongoing cognitive state. Would be grateful - polite conditional for a request, softer than "I am grateful to connect" (which would imply the connection already exists). Option D uses "was attending" (continuous) which implies you were interrupted mid-talk, and "am grateful" which sounds like the connection is already a done deal.

questions.q: You want to ask a connection if their company is hiring. Which message follows professional norms?
options: "Hi, I heard [Company] might be hiring. Do you know if that's true? Please let me know."
"Hey, is your company hiring? I'm looking for a new job ASAP."

"Hi [Name], I noticed your team recently shipped the distributed cache layer - impressive work. I've been following [Company]'s engineering blog for a year and your approach to consistency trade-offs resonates with my own work at [Current Company]. Are there open roles on your infrastructure team? Happy to share my CV."
"Hi, I'm very interested in working at [Company]. Can you refer me to your HR department? Thanks."
questions.explanation: Job inquiries through a connection work best when you demonstrate genuine interest in their specific work, show domain fit, and make a scoped, easy-to-answer ask . Option C: acknowledges a specific recent technical achievement (the cache layer), shows sustained engagement (following the blog for a year), connects their work to your own expertise, makes a specific ask (infrastructure team roles), and offers something in return (CV ready). Option B is abrupt and leads with urgency. Option A asks the connection to do investigative work on your behalf. Option D treats the connection as a routing mechanism, skipping the relationship entirely.

questions.q: Which subject line or opening is most effective for a cold networking email (not LinkedIn)?
options: "Hi, I found your email on your GitHub profile"
"Re: your article on WASM component model in InfoQ - a question about the compilation pipeline"
"Introduction from a fellow software engineer"
"Networking opportunity"
questions.explanation: A cold email subject line must give the recipient a reason to open it. Option B references a specific piece of work they produced (the InfoQ article), signals that the sender read it seriously enough to have a specific question (compilation pipeline), and provides context for why the sender is reaching out. This gives the recipient something they care about - a question about their own published work. Option D is generic and sounds like spam. Option C says nothing about who you are or why they should care. Option A is a statement of how you found their email - interesting as context but terrible as an opener since it creates privacy concerns.

questions.q: Choose the best phrasing for a follow-up after meeting at a conference: "It _____ (be) great _____ (meet) you at PyCon. I _____ (enjoy) our conversation about async IO patterns - I _____ (look) into the library you _____ (mention)."
options: was / to meet / enjoyed / am looking / mention
was / meeting / enjoyed / have been looking / mentioned
is / to meet / enjoy / have been looking / mentioned
was / to meet / enjoyed / looked / mentioned
questions.explanation: It was great meeting you - past simple + gerund ("meeting") is the standard English phrase for this context: "It was great + verb-ing". Enjoyed (past simple) - the conversation is a completed past event. Have been looking (present perfect continuous) - shows you started looking into the library after the conference and are still in the process. This signals ongoing, genuine follow-through. Mentioned (past simple) - refers to what was said during the conversation. Option D uses "to meet" (infinitive after "great") which is less natural here - the gerund is the idiomatic choice. "Am looking" (option A) would also work but present perfect continuous shows more concrete progress.

questions.q: David : 'Hey Sarah , just reviewing your PR for the new authentication module. Seems solid overall, but I'm a little concerned about the rate limiting logic - it might not handle peak loads effectively. Could you elaborate on your testing strategy?' Which LinkedIn message would be most appropriate for you to send to Sarah after this code review discussion? Consider building a longer-term relationship.
options: Insufficient - the PR needs immediate changes based solely on rate limiting concerns. Ignoring context.
Excellent - proactively offering detailed suggestions without acknowledging Sarah's perspective or asking for clarification.
Good - acknowledges the concern, invites further discussion about testing and scaling, and expresses willingness to collaborate. Focuses on a productive exchange .
Poor - simply restates the problem without any attempt to understand Sarah's reasoning or propose solutions.
questions.explanation: This question assesses your ability to transition a brief code review interaction into a networking opportunity. The correct answer demonstrates active listening and an invitation for deeper discussion-crucial for building rapport. Options A is too directive; B ignores the context of the conversation and fails to build a relationship. Option D simply repeats the problem without offering any engagement or collaboration. It's important to show you value Sarah's expertise and are open to learning from her .

questions.q: David recently provided feedback on your PR regarding authentication. You want to connect with him on LinkedIn to continue the conversation and potentially collaborate in the future. Which message is most appropriate?
options: 'Thanks for the feedback, David. Let's connect.'
'Hi David, just wanted to say thanks for the review!',
'David, great work on the authentication module!'
'Hey David, I appreciate your thoroughness on the PR. I'm particularly interested in discussing the rate limiting strategy further - could you share some resources?'
questions.explanation: Option B is too brief and doesn't show genuine interest in continuing the discussion. Option D demonstrates a proactive approach by specifically referencing his concerns and inviting further dialogue - this shows you were paying attention and value his expertise. Options A and C are generic and lack any substance for building a relationship. It's important to acknowledge specific feedback when networking, rather than just offering a general thanks.

I'm already working on it - thanks for the heads-up!

questions.q: You're a DevOps engineer and need to briefly explain the impact of increased latency during a stand-up meeting. Complete the sentence: 'We've been seeing some elevated latency in the API gateway, primarily due to _____ , which is impacting user experience.'
options: a recent database upgrade
increased traffic volume during peak hours
an unexpected surge in outbound network requests
server resource contention
questions.explanation: The most relevant reason for increased latency in an API gateway scenario is typically high traffic volume. Options A, B, and C are all plausible but less directly related to the immediate impact on user experience compared to a surge in requests. Framing it as 'increased traffic' helps the team understand the root cause quickly.

exercises.title: Meeting Agendas
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - writing agenda items, structuring technical meetings, pre-meeting notes, and time-check language.

questions.q: Which meeting agenda item is written correctly?
options: "Talk about the database migration and what we should do about it. 15 minutes."
"Review Q3 database migration plan - decide: proceed with rolling migration or full maintenance window? Owner: @priya. Time: 15 min."
"Database"
"Database migration discussion (important)"
questions.explanation: A well-written agenda item answers: what will be discussed , what decision needs to be made , who owns it , and how long it will take . Option B is specific about the topic (Q3 database migration plan), explicitly frames the decision (rolling vs. maintenance window), names an owner (@priya), and has a time box (15 min). Option C is a single word - it gives no context. Option A has no decision framing and is informal ("talk about"). Option D adds "(important)" as if any agenda item would be unimportant - the label adds no information.

questions.q: Complete the agenda intro: "This meeting _____ (aim) to _____ (reach) a decision on the caching strategy. By the end, we _____ (have) a chosen approach and a list of next steps. Please _____ (read) the RFC document before _____ (join)."
options: aims / reaching / will have / read / to join
is aiming / reaching / have / read / joining
will aim / reach / have / to read / joining
aims / reach / will have / read / joining
questions.explanation: Aims (present simple) describes the meeting's purpose as a designed fact. To reach - after "aim", English uses the to-infinitive: "aims to reach". Will have (future simple) - a concrete outcome promised by the end of the meeting. Read (base form imperative) - giving a pre-meeting instruction. Joining - after "before", use the gerund (verb-ing): "before joining". Option A uses "to join" (infinitive) after "before" which is grammatically wrong - "before" as a preposition must be followed by a gerund, not an infinitive. Option B uses "is aiming" which sounds like the meeting is currently in progress.

questions.q: Which set of agenda sections follows meeting best practices for a 1-hour technical design meeting?
options: 1. Welcome and introductions. 2. Discussion. 3. Next steps.

1. Context (5 min) - Why this design decision matters now. 2. Proposal walkthrough (15 min) - @alex presents RFC-12. 3. Open Q&A (15 min). 4. Decision (10 min) - Choose between Option A and Option B. 5. Action items (10 min) - Assign owners and deadlines. 6. Buffer (5 min).
1. Previous meeting recap. 2. Today's topic. 3. AOB (any other business).
1. Agenda review. 2. Main discussion. 3. Summary.
questions.explanation: A good technical meeting agenda uses time-boxed sections with named owners, a clear purpose, and an explicit decision point . Option B: every section has a time box (5/15/15/10/10/5), owners are named (RFC-12, @alex), the decision is explicitly framed (choose between A and B), action items are a dedicated section (not afterthought), and a buffer exists. Option A is typical of meetings that have no agenda - "Discussion" is not an agenda item. Option C uses "AOB" (Any Other Business) which is a trap - it becomes a dumping ground that derails timing. Option D is circular - "agenda review" at the start of the agenda serves no purpose.

questions.q: You are sending a meeting invite for a sprint retrospective. Which pre-meeting note is most useful?
options: "Please think about what went well and what didn't. No preparation required."
"Looking forward to a productive retro! See you then."
"Please come prepared to discuss the sprint."
"Before the meeting: (1) Add 2-3 items to the FunRetro board under Start/Stop/Continue (link below). (2) Skim the sprint velocity chart (link). We'll use both in the first 10 minutes."
questions.explanation: Pre-meeting notes should give attendees specific, actionable preparation tasks with links and context on how those inputs will be used . Option D: numbered tasks (clear count), specific actions (add 2-3 items to FunRetro), format guidance (Start/Stop/Continue), a link to the board, a second task (velocity chart), and timing context (used in first 10 min - so attendees know it matters immediately). Option C is too vague. Option B is a social nicety with no content. Option A contradicts itself: "no preparation required" cancels the instruction to "think about" things.

questions.q: Choose the correct phrasing for a time-check during a meeting: "We _____ (have) about 5 minutes left on this item. _____ (be) there any final points before we _____ (move) on? If we _____ (not/reach) consensus now, I _____ (suggest) we _____ (table) it for async follow-up."
options: have / Are / move / don't reach / suggest / table
are having / Is / move / won't reach / would suggest / table
had / Are / move / don't reach / suggest / table
have / Are / will move / don't reach / suggest / will table
questions.explanation: We have (present simple) for a current, factual time statement. Are there - plural question form ("points" is plural). Before we move on - present simple in the before-clause (not "will move"). If we don't reach - present simple in the if-clause (zero/first conditional: if + present simple, … present/will). I suggest - present simple for a real-time procedural suggestion. We table - after "suggest" + that-clause, English uses the base form (subjunctive): "I suggest we table it" not "I suggest we will table it". Option D uses "will move" in the before-clause which is wrong. Option B uses "is there" (singular) but "points" is plural.

questions.q: Liam sent the following Slack message to the team before a code review: 'Okay, let's look at this PR. The main issue is the data validation logic - it's not robust enough. Can everyone focus on that during the review?' Which of the following agenda items would be MOST appropriate for Sarah to add *immediately* after Liam's message to ensure a productive code review discussion?
options: Add an agenda item specifically addressing 'Robust Data Validation' and outlining the key areas for review.
Schedule a follow-up meeting to discuss data validation in detail.
Request a detailed breakdown of the current data validation implementation from Liam .
Post a link to relevant documentation on data validation best practices.
questions.explanation: The core issue identified by Liam (lack of robust data validation) needs immediate prioritization. Option C is correct because requesting a breakdown forces the team to directly address the problem and understand the specifics. Options B and D are less immediate; scheduling a follow-up or providing documentation doesn't tackle the *current* discussion point. This demonstrates how to quickly surface critical issues during a code review - it's about focusing the conversation, not just providing background information.

questions.q: Sarah is drafting the agenda for a sprint planning meeting. Which of these statements best describes the purpose of including a 'Risk Assessment' section? It's crucial to proactively identify potential roadblocks and develop mitigation strategies before the sprint begins, ensuring the team stays on track and minimizes disruptions .
options: Incorrect - a dedicated 'Risk Assessment' section is unnecessary for sprint planning.
Correct - to formally document all identified risks and their associated owners.
Incorrect - risk assessments are only relevant during emergencies.
Insufficient - simply listing risks without action items.
questions.explanation: The primary goal of a risk assessment in sprint planning isn't just listing potential problems. It's to proactively identify them, assign ownership for mitigation, and establish contingency plans - this demonstrates a strategic approach to sprint success. Option D is insufficient because it lacks the action-oriented element; options C and A misrepresent the role of risk assessments.

questions.q: You're preparing a Slack message to announce the agenda for tomorrow's code review meeting. Write a concise (under 50 words) message that clearly states the focus and expected outcomes. Use appropriate phrasing for requesting attention.
options: Incorrect - uses overly technical jargon.
Insufficient - doesn't specify what needs to be reviewed.
Incorrect - too verbose and lacks clarity.
Correct - 'Hi team, agenda: performance issues in Module X. Let's aim to identify root causes & propose solutions.'
questions.explanation: A well-crafted Slack message for a meeting agenda should be direct and informative. The example provided clearly states the topic (Module X), outlines the desired outcomes (root causes & solutions) and includes a polite request for attention. Option C is too long; options B and A lack essential details.

questions.q: During a technical design meeting, David sends the following message in the shared document: 'Let's discuss the API endpoint design. We need to ensure it adheres to version 2.0 specifications and handles at least 10,000 requests per second.' Which of the following best reflects how this information should be incorporated into the agenda? Consider the level of detail needed for a design discussion
options: Incorrect - omitting performance considerations from the agenda.
Insufficient - simply stating requirements without context.
Incorrect - including only technical specifications without considering user experience.
Correct - adding 'API Endpoint Design & Performance Requirements (v2.0, 10k RPS)' to the agenda.
questions.explanation: For a design meeting, it's crucial to clearly articulate the requirements and constraints. Adding 'API Endpoint Design & Performance Requirements (v2.0, 10k RPS)' provides context and directs the discussion effectively. Option B is too vague; options A and C miss key elements of the design process.

questions.q: Mark needs to update his team during a daily standup. Which sentence would be most appropriate for conveying that there's an agenda item regarding the upcoming database migration? Focus on clarity and action orientation
options: Insufficient - stating the topic without indicating its importance.
Incorrect - a lengthy explanation is always best for standups.
Incorrect - simply saying 'Database migration' doesn't provide sufficient information.
Correct - 'We'll be discussing the planned database migration in detail, aiming to finalize the rollback strategy.'
questions.explanation: Standup updates should be concise and action-oriented. This response clearly states the topic (database migration), outlines the goal (finalize rollback strategy) and sets expectations for further discussion. Option A is too vague; options B and C are inappropriate for a standup format.

questions.q: You're writing the PR description for a code change that fixes a bug. Which of the following phrases best describes how to incorporate agenda items into your PR description? Focus on context and impact
options: Incorrect - focusing solely on the code implementation details.
Incorrect - omitting any reference to previous discussions.
Insufficient - simply describing the technical fix without relating it to broader goals.
Correct - 'This resolves issue #123 (as discussed in yesterday's meeting) by implementing [code changes].'
questions.explanation: A PR description should provide context and highlight the impact of the change. Referencing a previous discussion (issue #123) connects the fix to the larger agenda and provides valuable information for reviewers. Option C is too narrow; options B and A lack crucial connections.

exercises.title: Meeting Follow-up Emails
exercises.subtitle: Practise the IT-English phrasing of meeting follow-up emails: recapping decisions, action items, owners and next steps.

questions.q: Which opening best 'recaps' a meeting concisely?
options: As discussed at length yesterday in great detail...
Thanks all - quick recap of what we agreed and the next steps below.
Why weren't you listening?
No summary needed.
questions.explanation: A brief recap framing plus a clear list is the standard, efficient follow-up structure.

questions.q: A follow-up lists 'action items' with owners. Why include an owner per item?
options: To assign blame
So it's clear who is responsible for each task
To make it longer
To hide tasks
questions.explanation: Naming an owner per action item creates accountability and avoids tasks falling through the cracks.

questions.q: Which phrase best states a 'next step' with a deadline?
options: Sometime soon.
Maria to send the draft spec by Friday 5pm.
Eventually we'll do it.
No deadline.
questions.explanation: A specific owner, task and date make the next step actionable and trackable.

questions.q: Why confirm 'decisions made' in the follow-up?
options: To restart the debate
To create a shared written record so everyone aligns on what was agreed
To add filler
To impress the boss
questions.explanation: Recording decisions prevents later disagreement about what the meeting concluded.

questions.q: Which closing invites correction politely?
options: This is final, no replies.
Let me know if I've missed or misstated anything.
Don't reply.
You'd better agree.
questions.explanation: Inviting corrections keeps the record accurate and signals openness.

questions.q: David from the code review mentioned a potential performance bottleneck in the new API endpoint. You've just sent a follow-up email summarizing the discussion and action items. Which of the following sentences best reflects your intention when stating that Sarah is responsible for investigating this further? Consider: This isn't simply assigning blame, but clarifying ownership for resolution.
options: 'Sarah needs to look into David's concerns regarding the API endpoint.'
'David requested that Sarah investigate the potential performance issue with the new endpoint.'
'Sarah will be responsible for investigating the reported bottleneck in the /users endpoint.'
'Please ensure Sarah prioritizes examining the API endpoint for any performance problems raised by David.'
questions.explanation: The correct answer clearly assigns responsibility to Sarah while acknowledging the original request. Options A and D are too verbose or imply a demand rather than a collaborative task assignment. Option B is technically accurate but lacks direct ownership; it simply restates David's request without specifying who should act upon it. Focusing on clear ownership, as demonstrated in option 2, is key to effective follow-up emails.

questions.q: John from the sprint planning meeting highlighted a key challenge: integrating the new authentication service with our existing microservices. You've drafted a follow-up email summarizing the discussion and outlining next steps. Which sentence best communicates your intention when assigning Mike the task of creating a proof-of-concept integration? Consider: This isn't just delegating a small task, but clearly defining responsibility for a critical technical exploration.
options: Insufficient - Mike lacks experience with microservices.
Excellent - It directly assigns Mike to create the POC and sets expectations for success.
Acceptable - It states Mike will 'explore' integration options, which is vague.
Poor - Simply stating 'Mike should work on the integration' offers no guidance or accountability.
questions.explanation: The correct answer (Excellent) demonstrates an understanding of clear communication in a technical context. Assigning responsibility with a specific task (creating a proof-of-concept) is crucial for effective project management and avoids ambiguity. The other options are either too vague, assign blame unnecessarily, or fail to provide the necessary level of detail for Mike to understand his role.

questions.q: Alex from the Slack channel reported that the response time for the new user signup API was consistently slow during peak hours. You've drafted a follow-up email to the team summarizing the issue and assigning tasks. Which of the following sentences best clarifies Ben's role in addressing this concern?
options: Insufficient - simply stating Ben is responsible doesn't explain his specific contribution.
Excellent - clearly assigns Ben ownership, but lacks detail about *how* he should investigate.
Good - it establishes Ben as the point of contact for resolving the issue, which is a crucial first step.
Best - It explicitly defines what action Ben needs to take (e.g., 'Ben will analyze the API logs' or 'Ben will optimize the database query')
questions.explanation: The key here isn't just assigning ownership; it's about making sure Ben understands *what* is expected of him. Option A focuses on a lack of detail which is exactly what we need to avoid. Options B and C are too vague - 'responsible' doesn't convey action. Option D provides the necessary specificity, ensuring Ben knows how his work contributes to solving the problem. A good follow-up clarifies expectations, reducing ambiguity.

questions.q: Which welcome email subject line is most effective for a new software engineer joining the team?
options: Hi [Name]! 👋
Welcome!
Welcome to the team, [Name] - your first day checklist
New employee information
questions.explanation: "Welcome to the team, [Name] - your first day checklist" is most effective. Analysis: Personalised with name - immediately addresses the recipient directly "First day checklist" - tells the reader exactly what is inside; they know to read this before starting Option B ("Welcome!") is too vague - no context for a busy inbox Option D is impersonal and bureaucratic Option A with emoji may be fine in casual cultures, but is risky in professional contexts and gives no useful information

questions.q: You are writing first-day instructions for a new backend engineer. Which paragraph structure is most useful?
options: A list of tools and links with no explanation of what to do with them.
Numbered steps: 1. Set up your dev environment. 2. Read the onboarding wiki. 3. Attend the 10am team standup. 4. Message your buddy by EOD.
A short note saying "Check with your buddy for next steps."
A long paragraph covering system access, team norms, first tasks, and key contacts all together.
questions.explanation: Numbered steps with specific, actionable items are most useful for first-day instructions. Key principles: Numbered list - creates a clear order of priority and allows the new hire to track progress Specific tasks - "Attend the 10am standup" beats "Join the team meeting" (which meeting? what time?) Single action per step - one thing per numbered item prevents overwhelm Option D (long paragraph) is hard to scan under first-day stress Option A (links without context) leaves the new hire guessing Option C puts all responsibility on the buddy and gives no structure

questions.q: You are assigning a buddy to a new hire. Which buddy assignment email best sets clear expectations?
options: Hi Priya, I'd like to assign you as buddy for Tomás, who joins us on Monday. Could you schedule a 30-minute intro call in his first week and be his go-to for informal questions?
Priya, you're assigned as buddy for Tomás. Let me know if that works.
Hi Priya, Tomás is joining. Please help him out.
Hey Priya, can you be Tomás's buddy? Thanks!
questions.explanation: Option A sets clear expectations correctly. It includes: The name and start date - "Tomás, who joins us on Monday" A specific deliverable - "schedule a 30-minute intro call in his first week" The scope of the role - "go-to for informal questions" (not "everything," which causes scope creep) Option D is too casual and has no specifics. Option B assigns without explaining responsibilities. Option C ("help him out") is so vague it creates no clear commitment.

questions.q: A new hire emails you: "I'm not sure who to ask about getting a VPN token set up." Which redirect email is most helpful?
options: Ask IT.
Please raise a ticket with the IT helpdesk at helpdesk@company.com - the SLA for access provisioning is 1 business day. CC your line manager so they can prioritise if needed.
Good question! I think it's the IT team. Try reaching out to them.
VPN tokens are handled by IT ops - ask your buddy.
questions.explanation: Option B gives a complete, actionable redirect. It includes: A specific contact method - "raise a ticket at helpdesk@company.com" (not just "ask IT") The expected timeline - "SLA for access provisioning is 1 business day" sets expectations A practical tip - CC your manager for prioritisation tells the new hire how to escalate if needed Options A, C, and D all point to "IT" without giving the new hire what they need to actually take action. A good onboarding redirect always includes: who + how to contact + what to expect.

questions.q: Which closing line is most appropriate for a new-hire welcome email from a team lead?
options: We're genuinely glad to have you on the team. Your first standup is Monday at 10am - see you there.
Good luck!
Welcome aboard! Looking forward to working with you.
Let me know if you have any questions!
questions.explanation: "We're genuinely glad to have you on the team. Your first standup is Monday at 10am - see you there." combines warmth with a concrete next step. Analysis: Personal warmth - "genuinely glad" sounds human, not corporate-boilerplate Specific next action - "Monday at 10am standup" removes the anxiety of "what do I do first?" Option D ("Let me know if you have any questions!") is kind but passive - new hires often don't know what questions to ask yet Option C is fine but generic - every company says "looking forward to working with you" Option B ("Good luck!") implies uncertainty - not what a new hire wants to hear

questions.q: PR Description Sarah just submitted a PR to fix a critical bug in the authentication service. She's included a detailed explanation of the issue and her proposed solution. Which of the following descriptions is MOST effective for reviewers, considering best practices for code review feedback?
options: "This PR addresses a high-priority authentication vulnerability. The fix involves updating the token validation logic in AuthService.validateToken() to account for the recent API changes. Please ensure thorough testing of the updated logic, especially concerning edge cases."
"Please review this PR - it fixes a bug!"
"This PR is ready for review. It's a small fix that should be easy to merge."
"Just reviewing this code - let me know if you have any questions!"
questions.explanation: The best option clearly communicates the severity of the issue (high-priority vulnerability), specifies exactly which code needs reviewing ( AuthService.validateToken() ), and asks for targeted testing - this is crucial for efficient code review. Options B and A are too vague, while option D isn't specific enough to guide reviewers effectively. Option C minimizes the value of a code review by suggesting it's 'easy to merge' without proper scrutiny.

questions.q: David , the new frontend developer, posted a message in Slack: 'Just got stuck on the API response format for the user profile endpoint. Getting `400 Bad Request` errors. Any ideas?' Which response is MOST appropriate for your team lead to send immediately?
options: 'Have you tried refreshing the page? Sometimes that fixes these issues.'
'Okay, David, let's troubleshoot this. Can you share the exact API response you're receiving?'
'Sounds like a problem with the request data! Double-check your payload.'
'That's normal for new users - the API sometimes needs a little time to initialize.'
questions.explanation: The best response directly asks for actionable information - the specific API response. This moves beyond vague suggestions and allows for targeted troubleshooting. Option C is too general, option B demonstrates helpful guidance, and options D & A are unhelpful distractions or assumptions.

questions.q: You're drafting a PR description for a fix to a performance bottleneck in the database query. The fix involves adding an index. Which of the following sentences is MOST effective for summarizing this change?
options: 'We've added an index to improve database access speed, addressing a significant slowdown.'
'This resolves a minor issue with the database connection.'
'The code was refactored for better readability.'
'This commit optimizes query performance.'
questions.explanation: Option 1 clearly and concisely explains *why* the change was made (performance optimization) and what was done (adding an index). Options D & A are too vague, while option C misrepresents the purpose of adding an index. Option B is completely irrelevant.

questions.q: Maria, a new DevOps engineer, sends you an email saying: 'I'm trying to deploy my application using Kubernetes, but I keep getting errors related to service discovery. I've checked the network policies and DNS configuration.' Which of the following is the BEST follow-up question to ask her?
options: 'Can you share the full error message and the current state of your Kubernetes deployment?'
'Are you using a specific version of kubectl?'
'Did you consult the official Kubernetes documentation?'
'Have you restarted your cluster?'
questions.explanation: Requesting the full error message and deployment state provides the most crucial context for diagnosing the problem. While other options touch on potential issues, they don't directly solicit the information needed to understand the root cause of the service discovery errors.

questions.q: You are writing an onboarding email for a new security engineer. Which statement best explains the importance of regularly reviewing code?
options: 'Code reviews are primarily about identifying bugs and fixing them quickly.'
'Code reviews are a formality to comply with company policies.'
'Frequent code reviews help detect security vulnerabilities early in the development lifecycle, preventing potential breaches.'
'Regular code reviews ensure that all developers follow best practices.'
questions.explanation: While regular code reviews *do* contribute to best practices and bug identification, option 2 accurately highlights their core purpose in security: proactively finding vulnerabilities. Options D & A focus on secondary benefits, while option B misrepresents the critical role of code reviews in a security context.

questions.q: You are drafting a closing statement for an email to a new team member. Which of the following is MOST appropriate?
options: 'Good luck with your first project.'
'Let me know if you have any questions.'
'Please don't hesitate to reach out for support - we're here to help you succeed.'
'We're excited to have you on board!'
questions.explanation: Option 2 expresses genuine enthusiasm and welcomes the new team member. It's a friendly and positive closing that reinforces the welcoming tone of the onboarding process. The other options are too generic or focused on future tasks.

exercises.title: 📬 Email Phrase Bank
exercises.subtitle: 40 ready-to-use phrases covering every stage of a professional IT email - from opening to sign-off. Bookmark this page. Then test yourself with the 5 exercises below.

questions.q: You received an important email on Monday but couldn't reply until Thursday. Which phrase from the bank is the most professional opener for your response?
options: "I apologise for the delay in responding."
"Looking forward to your feedback."
"Just to confirm, I have received your email."
"This is a gentle reminder that…"
questions.explanation: "I apologise for the delay in responding." - When replying late, acknowledge the delay first , before addressing the email's content. This signals professional awareness and courtesy. Why the others don't fit: • "Just to confirm, I have received your email" - this is for when you've just received an email; using it 3 days later would be odd • "Looking forward to your feedback" - a closing phrase, not an opener • "This is a gentle reminder" - used when YOU are following up on THEM; here they've been waiting on YOU Full example: "I apologise for the delay in responding - I was at the team offsite this week. Here's the information you requested:…"

questions.q: A vendor hasn't responded to your last two emails about a contract renewal. It's now urgent. Which combination of phrases from the bank builds the most effective follow-up?
options: "As discussed in our last meeting" + "Please let me know if you have any questions."
"I apologise for the delay" + "Could you confirm that you've received this?"
"I wanted to follow up on my previous email" + "This is a gentle reminder that the contract renewal is due next week."
"I'm writing to inform you" + "We're unable to accommodate this request at this time."
questions.explanation: "I wanted to follow up" + "gentle reminder with deadline" - the correct combination for a second-contact chase. Why it works: ① "I wanted to follow up on my previous email" - signals a repeated contact without aggression ② "This is a gentle reminder that the contract renewal is due next week" - adds urgency; "gentle" is a professional hedging word that keeps the tone polite, not threatening Why the others fail: • "As discussed in our last meeting" - if they're ignoring emails, there was probably no recent meeting; this phrase assumes shared context that isn't there • "I apologise for the delay" - here THEY are the unresponsive party; you don't apologise for their silence

questions.q: A product manager sent a last-minute request to add a feature to the current sprint. You can't do it but want to keep the relationship positive. Which phrase is most appropriate?
options: "I'm afraid our capacity is fully committed until end of sprint."
"We're unable to accommodate this request at this time."
"This falls outside the scope of the current sprint."
"I'd suggest deprioritising this for now and revisiting it in the next sprint planning."
questions.explanation: "I'd suggest deprioritising this for now and revisiting it in the next sprint planning." Why this is best: • Frames as a prioritisation decision , not a hard refusal - "not now" rather than "no" • "I'd suggest" is collaborative - invites agreement • "Next sprint planning" is a concrete, specific future moment - not a vague "later" • Keeps the working relationship with the PM positive Why the others are weaker: • "We're unable to accommodate" - closes the conversation; no future alternative offered • "Falls outside the scope" - accurate but sounds bureaucratic and distant • "Capacity is fully committed" - fine, but more formal than needed for a peer PM conversation Tip: When declining a stakeholder request, always name a specific time for the revisit.

questions.q: Your CTO needs to approve a server migration plan by Friday or the project will slip by three weeks. Which phrase communicates the urgency most effectively?
options: "I wanted to flag this as something to look at when you have a moment."
"Just checking in on the status of the server migration approval."
"We need a decision on this by Friday to avoid a three-week timeline slip."
"I'm reaching out regarding the migration plan."
questions.explanation: "We need a decision on this by Friday to avoid a three-week timeline slip." This is from the Escalating & Flagging Urgency group. It's the most effective because it contains all three elements of a well-formed urgency message: ① Clear ask : "we need a decision" ② Concrete deadline : "by Friday" ③ Quantified consequence : "three-week timeline slip" Why the others fail at urgency: • "Just checking in" - signals LOW priority; no urgency • "I'm reaching out regarding" - neutral opener with no urgency • "when you have a moment" - actively signals low priority; the opposite of urgency Formula: [Clear ask] + [Deadline] + [Consequence of not acting] = effective escalation.

questions.q: You have resolved a P1 incident affecting the payments service. You need to send a brief update to the team. Which combination of phrases is most appropriate?
options: "Looking forward to your feedback" + "I can confirm that the issue has been resolved."
"I apologise for the delay" + "Feel free to reach out if you need anything else."
"This is to confirm that the issue has been resolved." + "Please let me know if you have any questions."
"This is to confirm that the issue has been resolved." + "I'll keep you posted as things develop."
questions.explanation: "This is to confirm that the issue has been resolved." + "Please let me know if you have any questions." Why this is best: ① "This is to confirm that the issue has been resolved" - definitive, professional resolution statement from the Confirming & Acknowledging group; signals certainty ② "Please let me know if you have any questions" - standard professional closing; invites follow-up questions without creating ambiguity Why option D is wrong: "I'll keep you posted as things develop" implies the situation is ongoing . After a resolution, this creates confusion about whether the fix is final. Why option A is wrong: "Looking forward to your feedback" implies you're asking for something from them. After resolving an incident, you're delivering an update - not seeking feedback on your work. Tip: Incident resolution communications should be definitive. Avoid anything that suggests the situation might continue.

questions.q: Sarah : 'The API is returning a 500 error. We need to investigate.' Mark (your teammate) replies in Slack: 'Okay, let's debug it. Any initial thoughts?' Which of the following phrases would be the most professional and actionable response from you, building on Mark's question?
options: Insufficient - merely stating the error doesn't convey urgency or a plan.
'500 errors are always tricky. Can you share the full API response?' - This directly seeks more information and starts a diagnostic process.
'I've checked the logs; there seems to be an issue with the database connection. Let's try reconnecting.'
'That's great, let me know if you need any help!' - A generic acknowledgement is fine in this situation.
questions.explanation: The key here is to move beyond simply stating the problem (the 500 error). While acknowledging the issue is important, a professional developer response should immediately demonstrate proactive investigation. Option 3 asks for the full API response - a crucial step in debugging - and initiates a collaborative diagnostic process. Options A and C are passive or lack actionable steps; option D is overly dismissive.
